articles.title: Other people's work
articles.standfirst: Why a small project spends its time pointing at 122 books and 23 films instead of summarising them.
body: There is a version of this project that would have been much faster to build. Read the scholarship, absorb it, and republish it in shorter sentences under this site's own name. Nobody would have noticed, most sites on most subjects work exactly that way, and it would have produced a great deal more text a great deal sooner.

This site does the opposite thing, and the reading room and the watch room are where that choice is most visible. 122 books across 11 shelves. 23 films, lectures and recordings. In neither case does this site summarise the work and send you away satisfied. It tells you what the thing is, why it is worth your time, and exactly where to get it.

The reason is not modesty. It is that summaries of scholarship are the least reliable objects on the internet, and a summary of a summary is worse. Every step away from the original loses the qualifications, the disputed points, the footnote where the author says the evidence is thinner than the chapter title suggests. By the third retelling, a careful scholar's hedged claim has become a confident fact on a hundred pages, and there is no way back to the hedge. This subject is unusually prone to it, because the source material is scattered, the communities are small, and almost nobody checks.

So the rule here is that when somebody else has done the work properly, the useful thing to do is to name them, say what they did, and get out of the way. Nathan Katz wrote the standard overview of all three historic communities. Jael Silliman built the Calcutta archive. Johanna Spector filmed the Konkan villages in the 1970s while there were still people in them to film. This project cannot improve on any of that and has no business paraphrasing it.

What a project like this can add is the connective tissue. Nobody had put those 122 books in one place with a working link on each. Nobody had assembled the films with a line on each saying what it actually contains rather than what its title promises. Nobody had built a sourced list of the buildings. Those are unglamorous jobs and they are the jobs that were open.

There is a second rule underneath the first, which is about copyright and is less philosophical. Almost everything worth reading on this subject is in copyright, held by living authors or by their estates, and a good deal of it is published by small presses that keep this material in print at commercial risk. Reproducing a poem or a chapter here would take money out of the hands of the people who did the work, in exchange for making this site look fuller. That is a bad trade even when it is legal, and often it is not legal.

This is why the poetry on this site is discussed and not printed. Readers have asked for the poems themselves, and the answer is no, with one exception this project is glad to make: where a full text is genuinely free and legally available, the reading room links straight to it and marks it. 9 of the 122 books are in that category. For everything else, the link goes to a catalogue where you can find a copy, and buying one is a more useful form of support for this field than anything this project can offer.

The same logic governs the watch room. The films are not re-hosted, re-cut or downloaded. Each entry names the channel that published it, and pressing play loads it from YouTube, through the no cookie domain, and not before you press. Nobody's work is taken and nobody's viewing figures are stolen, which matters when several of these films were made by tiny operations documenting a community that will not be documentable much longer.

The test this project applies before adding anything to either room is simple enough to state in one line. Would somebody who followed this link be glad they did, and does the link still work? The second half of that is not a formality. A reading list where a third of the links are dead is worse than no reading list, because it wastes the reader's time and then makes them doubt everything else on the page.

articles.title: What remains standing
articles.standfirst: Thirteen buildings, four communities, four hundred years, and a pattern that repeats until it stops looking like a coincidence.
body: This piece analyses the built heritage survey on this site. It asserts nothing that is not already in that directory with a source attached, and where the directory records a gap, this piece records the same gap rather than smoothing it over. The principal source underneath most of it is Synagogues360, published by ANU, the Museum of the Jewish People. Dates of construction and statements of present condition are as recorded there.

Start with the arithmetic, because it is unflattering. The directory holds thirteen sites. Five of those thirteen have no recorded construction date, and the same five are marked incomplete, meaning this project has the building's name and not much else. That is a survey with more than a third of its entries unfinished, and saying so in the first paragraph is the only honest way to begin.

Now the part that is finished. The oldest entry is the Paradesi Synagogue in Kochi, built in 1568 by the city's Jewish trading community, including Sephardic families exiled from Spain and Portugal, in the settlement the community established after relocating from Kodungallur in 1524. The newest is Judah Hyam Hall in New Delhi, whose foundation stone was laid on 12 February 1956 and which was completed on 2 September 1956. Between those two dates lie three hundred and eighty-eight years and the entire built history of Jewish India that this project has so far been able to source.

Four hundred years is not a long time for a religious architecture. What makes this record unusual is how much of it is concentrated into a single century. Shaar Harahamim in Mumbai dates to 1796. Shaare Rason follows in 1840 or 1843, the source giving both. Magen David is 1861 and Keneseth Eliyahoo is 1884. Four of the thirteen sites, and the four that anchor Jewish Bombay, go up inside eighty-eight years. That century is the century of the Bombay Presidency, of the Sassoon fortune, and of a Bene Israel community moving off the Konkan coast and into the city.

The two Bombay Bene Israel synagogues in that run tell a story that has nothing to do with imperial commerce. Shaar Harahamim, the oldest Bene Israel synagogue in India, was founded by Samuel Ezekiel Divekar, recorded in the source under the alternative name Samaji Hasaji Divekar, a battalion commandant who, according to the account the source carries, resolved to build a synagogue if he survived capture by Mysore forces in May 1796. Forty-odd years later, a group broke away from that congregation and built Shaare Rason a short distance away. A community small enough to have one synagogue in 1796 is not small enough to avoid a schism by 1840. That is a fact about the internal life of the Bene Israel, and it is legible in the building record without any narrative being added to it.

Then the Sassoons arrive. David Sassoon, head of the family that reached Bombay in 1832, built Magen David in 1861 in a Neo Classical style, and put a Torah school on the grounds that his son expanded in 1910. His sons Jacob Elias and Albert built Keneseth Eliyahoo in 1884, in Victorian style, in memory of their father. The pattern worth noticing is that the Baghdadi institutional footprint in Bombay ran to schools, hospitals and libraries as much as to synagogues. A trading family that endows a school next to a synagogue is not only building for worship. It is building for permanence.
The permanence did not hold, and the directory records how it failed, building by building, in a sequence that is the single most useful thing in the whole dataset.

The sequence goes: the congregation leaves, then the scrolls leave, then the interior leaves, and the building stays. Kadavumbagam in Ernakulam is the clearest case. It ceased functioning as an active synagogue in 1972. The Torah scrolls were shipped to the Cochin National Heritage Center in 1974. In 1991 the interior and the Aron Kodesh were transported to Moshav Nehalim in Israel for restoration. The front building now houses a business, and the guardian permits visitors to see the grounds. Four thousand kilometres now separate the shell from its contents.

Parur, built in 1615, shows the same movement on a shorter timescale. Its original bimah and Aron Kodesh were shipped to Israel in 1995 and replaced with reconstructions. Restoration of the building itself began in 2009, and the source, written at the time, projected completion in spring 2011. So the building is being restored in Kerala while its original fittings sit in Israel. Both halves are being cared for. Neither is whole.

It is worth being precise about what this pattern is and is not. It is not destruction. Nothing in this directory was burned, bulldozed or seized. It is not neglect either, in most cases: Parur was restored, Keneseth Eliyahoo is active and well maintained, and Shaar Harahamim runs daily services in a building that seats three hundred for a congregation of roughly a hundred. What the pattern actually is, is the physical trace of a migration. The fittings went where the people went. That is what a community moving looks like when you can only see the buildings.

Parur also carries the architectural point that most general accounts of Indian Jewish heritage miss. The complex comprises seven buildings, built of whitewashed lime and laterite with terracotta tile roofing, in the manner of Kerala architecture rather than of any imported synagogue form. Ten large shuttered windows on the walls are read as the Ten Commandments. That is a Jewish idea executed in a Kerala building tradition, by builders working in the Thachusasthra tradition, which is what the source records for it. The Paradesi Synagogue gets the visitors and the photographs. Parur is the more interesting building.

One entry in the directory belongs to a different century and a different problem. Judah Hyam Hall in New Delhi is the newest building in the survey by more than seventy years, and the only one built after Indian independence. It serves roughly fifty local members along with diplomats and visitors. Its practice departs from custom in ways the source states plainly: the rabbi has never been ordained, the doors are open to people of all faiths, and women count towards the ten people required for a service. That last one is not a small adjustment. It is the kind of change a congregation makes when the alternative is not being able to hold a service at all.

So the directory contains at least three different kinds of Jewish history, and they do not resolve into one story. There is a seventeenth century Kerala trading community building in the local vernacular. There is a nineteenth century Baghdadi commercial dynasty building for permanence in an imperial port. There is a twentieth century capital city congregation of fifty people rewriting the rules in order to survive. Flattening these into one narrative about the Jews of India would lose everything that is actually interesting about them.

Five entries in the directory exist mainly as a rebuke to this project. Ohel David in Pune, known as the Red Synagogue, is named by the World Jewish Congress among notable Jewish places in India. This site has not verified a construction date for it and will not print one until it has, even though a date is easy enough to find repeated in half a dozen places online. Tiphereth Israel in Mumbai, Shaar Hashamaim in Thane, and Mala and Chennamangalam in Kerala are listed by name and almost nothing more. All five are in the directory because leaving them out would make the survey look more complete than it is.

There is one more gap, and it is the largest one. Every site in this directory is in Maharashtra, Kerala or Delhi. Gujarat is absent, and the Bene Israel presence in Ahmedabad is documented elsewhere on this site without a single building recorded for it. West Bengal is absent, although the Baghdadi community of Kolkata appears in the register of people, in the culture pages and in the watch room. The north east is absent entirely. A survey of Jewish built heritage in India covering three states is a start rather than a survey, and the honest name for what is on this site is a working directory.

The reason to keep building it is that no complete, machine readable, sourced list of these buildings exists anywhere. That is a strange thing to be true in 2026 about a body of architecture spanning four centuries, but it is true, and it is the gap this project is most likely to be able to close. The buildings are the part of this history that physically remains. Everything else, the congregations, the languages, the liturgy, the arguments between congregations, is either in Israel now or in living memory, and living memory is a wasting asset.

If you can add a building, a date, a photograph taken by you, or a present condition, with a source, this project wants it. That is not a formality at the end of an article. Five of thirteen entries are missing their dates, and the fastest way that number comes down is somebody who lives near one of these buildings writing in.

articles.title: What the source register is made of
articles.standfirst: Ninety sources hold this site up. Here is what they are, what each kind can and cannot prove, and where the register is thin enough to worry about.
body: Every factual record on this site points at a source in a register, and a script refuses to publish if any record points at nothing or at something not in the register. That much is a mechanical guarantee and it is worth exactly what a mechanical guarantee is worth, which is less than most sites implying they have one would like you to think. A script can confirm that a claim has a source attached. It cannot confirm that the source says what the claim says it says, and it certainly cannot confirm that the source is right.
So the useful question is not whether this site has sources. It is what kind of sources, in what proportion, and with what blind spots. This piece answers that.

The register sorts every source into one of four tiers, and the tier is not a quality score. It is a statement about what kind of thing the source is, because different kinds of source can support different kinds of claim.

A primary source is the document itself or the body that produced it. A Ministry of External Affairs country brief, a Press Information Bureau release, a Prime Minister's Office statement, a United Nations General Assembly resolution record, a Defence Research and Development Organisation page about its own missile programme. When this site says India recognised Israel on 17 September 1950, the source is the Ministry of External Affairs brief that states it. That is the strongest kind of citation available for a fact of that type, and it is still only as good as the ministry's own record keeping.

A reference source is an encyclopaedia, a museum catalogue, an institutional database, an academic reference work. Britannica on the Paradesi Synagogue. The World Jewish Congress on the communities. Synagogues360, published by ANU, the Museum of the Jewish People, which is the backbone of the built heritage survey. These are secondary by definition. They are compiled by people who read the primary material, and they are usually right, and when they are wrong the error is invisible from the outside. This site treats a reference source as good enough to print and not good enough to be certain about.

A press source is journalism. Dated, attributed, and written on a deadline. Press citations here are used for events, announcements, figures given at a moment in time, and current conditions. They are the right source for what a minister said in a particular week and the wrong source for anything that requires the passage of time to assess.

A community source is the community's own account of itself. This tier exists because of one specific problem. The Bene Israel hold that their ancestors reached the Konkan coast roughly two thousand five hundred years ago after a shipwreck. That account is transmitted within the community and is central to how the community understands itself. It is not a dated document. Treating it as one would be dishonest, and dismissing it would be both rude and wrong, because a tradition maintained for centuries is evidence of something even when it is not evidence of the event it describes. So it goes in its own tier and is labelled, which is the only treatment that does not require lying in one direction or the other.

That last distinction is the one that matters most for a site about this subject, and it generalises. Migration numbers are a good example. Community organisations, government briefs and press reports routinely give different figures for how many Jews left India for Israel, and for how many people of Indian origin now live in Israel. Where this site has two figures from two credible sources, it shows both and names both, rather than averaging them or picking the one that reads better.
Now the weaknesses, which are the part of a methodology note that is actually worth reading.

First: the register leans heavily on a small number of workhorses. The Synagogues360 database carries most of the built heritage survey almost single handed. The World Jewish Congress country page carries a large share of the community claims. If either of those is wrong about something, this site is wrong about it too, and there is currently no independent check in place. That is a real single point of failure and it is not solved by adding more citations that all trace back to the same original.

Second: the register is thin before the eighteenth century. Everything this site can say about the first fifteen hundred years of Jewish presence in India rests on reference works and community tradition, because the primary material is copper plates, inscriptions and manuscripts that this project has not read in the original and cannot read in the original. The Kerala copper plates are real, dated and studied. This site cites accounts of them rather than the plates themselves, and that distinction should stay visible.

Third: the register is overweight on official Indian government sources for the modern relationship. Ministry briefs, Press Information Bureau releases and Prime Minister's Office statements are primary, they are precise about dates, and they are also promotional documents produced by one of the two parties. A joint statement tells you what two governments agreed to say. It does not tell you what they agreed to do, what they failed to agree, or what the meeting was actually about. Using them as the spine of a timeline is defensible. Using them as the whole of it is not, and this site currently does more of the second than it should.

Fourth: there is very little material in the register that is not in English, and very little Israeli official material. That is a limit of the person building it rather than a judgement about what exists. A relationship between two countries documented mainly in the English language output of one of them is documented at a slant. Anyone who can read the Israel State Archives, the Knesset record, or Judeo Marathi material and is willing to contribute citations would be more useful to this project than almost anything else.

Fifth: every source carries an accessed date, which is the day the link was checked. Links rot. Government reorganisations move briefs, newspapers move to archives behind paywalls, museums redesign their databases. A source that resolved in August 2026 may not resolve next year, and there is no mechanism here that will notice. The accessed date is at least an honest statement of when the claim was last standing on something real.

None of these five is a reason to distrust the site more than you would distrust any comparable one. They are a reason to know what you are reading. A research site that publishes its weaknesses is not confessing. It is telling you where to push.

One practical note for anyone using this material. Every source in the register carries a publisher, a title, a link, a tier and an accessed date, and the whole register can be exported as CSV or JSON from the open dataset page. If you are checking a claim on this site, the fastest route is to open the source line under it rather than searching for the claim elsewhere, because what you want to know first is not whether the claim is true. It is whether this site has read what it says it has read.

articles.title: The forty-two years
articles.standfirst: India recognised Israel in 1950 and exchanged embassies in 1992. Everything interesting about the relationship lives in the gap between those two dates.
body: Two dates are recorded in the Ministry of External Affairs brief on India and Israel. India recognised the State of Israel on 17 September 1950. Full diplomatic relations were established in 1992. Between them sit forty-two years.

Most popular accounts of the relationship treat 1992 as the beginning and skip the gap entirely. That is a mistake of framing rather than of fact. Recognition and diplomatic relations are two different acts. Recognition says a state exists. Diplomatic relations say two states will maintain permanent missions and conduct business through them. A country can do the first without the second for a very long time, and India did.

What this project can state from the primary record is narrow and worth stating precisely: the recognition happened in 1950, the relations happened in 1992, and the interval was forty-two years. The brief records the dates. It does not explain them.

The explanation is where the history actually is, and it is contested. Accounts of the period point to several factors operating at once: India's own position in the non aligned movement, its relationships across West Asia, the domestic politics of a large Muslim population, the Cold War alignment of the region, and the changing shape of all of this by the early 1990s. These are not equally weighted by every historian, and this project does not pretend to have settled the question.

What is worth noticing is the shape of the interval. Forty-two years is not a delay. It is longer than the entire modern relationship has so far lasted. Any account of India and Israel that begins in 1992 has cut off more than half the story, and has cut off precisely the half that explains why the second half looks the way it does.

There is a second thing the interval does. It makes the post 1992 acceleration legible as acceleration. Between 1992 and 2017, twenty-five years passed before an Indian Prime Minister visited Israel. Between 2017 and 2026, the record fills up: state visits in both directions, ministerial traffic in most years, a bilateral investment agreement, terms of reference for a free trade agreement, a defence cooperation memorandum, and repeated telephone contact at head of government level. Something changed in the tempo, and the forty-two years are the baseline against which that change can be measured.

This project's position is that the interval is the most under examined thing in the whole relationship, and that filling it in with sources is more valuable than adding another summary of the years after 1992. It is listed among the open questions for that reason.

articles.title: The evidence ladder
articles.standfirst: How this project decides what it is allowed to say, and what the labels on every page actually mean.
body: Every factual block on this site carries a label. The labels are not decoration and they are not a rating of how much the project likes a claim. They record what kind of evidence sits underneath it, which is a different question from whether it is true.

A primary source is a government document, a treaty, an official brief, a statement issued by a ministry, or a record produced by the institution that did the thing being described. The Ministry of External Affairs bilateral brief is a primary source. So is the Embassy of India's own page about the Indian community in Israel. Primary sources are not neutral, and they are not always right. A government brief describes what a government wants recorded. What makes it primary is that it is the institution speaking for itself, which is exactly the thing a researcher needs to be able to quote.

A reference source is an encyclopaedia entry, or a publication by an established institution whose business is compiling and checking. Britannica on the Paradesi Synagogue is a reference source. The World Jewish Congress on Jewish communities in India is a reference source. These are usually reliable and usually not the last word.

A press source is an established news organisation. Nothing on this site currently rests on a press source alone, and where the newsroom gathers headlines automatically they are marked as unverified until a person checks them.

A community claim is an account transmitted within a community about itself. The Bene Israel tradition of arrival on the Konkan coast around 2,500 years ago is a community claim. This label does not mean the claim is false and it does not mean it is unimportant. It means the evidence is of a different kind: memory carried forward rather than a document that can be dated. Communities are entitled to their own account of where they came from. A research site is obliged to say which kind of thing it is looking at.

There is a fifth label, and it is the one this project is most attached to: sources differ. When two credible sources give different figures, the honest move is to show both. Two Indian government sources give different numbers for the Indian origin population in Israel, and different numbers again for Indian citizens there. This site does not average them, pick the larger one, or pick the one from the more recent document. It shows both and names the gap as a research question.

The rule is enforced in code rather than by good intentions. Every record in the content files must carry at least one source identifier, and a check refuses to publish the site if any record does not. This is deliberately inconvenient. Inconvenience is the point: it makes adding an unsourced claim harder than adding a sourced one.

What this system cannot do should also be said. It does not verify that a source is correct, only that it exists and says what the page claims it says. It does not detect a claim that is true in its source and misleading in the way this site frames it. Those failures are caught by readers, which is why the corrections address sits on every page, and why corrections are published rather than quietly applied.

articles.title: Four communities, one careless label
articles.standfirst: The phrase 'Indian Jews' hides four distinct histories that arrive in different centuries, speak different languages, and leave for different reasons.
body: The Embassy of India in Tel Aviv lists the Jewish communities of Indian origin in Israel as the Bene Israel of Maharashtra, the Cochin Jews of Kerala, the Baghdadi Jews of Kolkata, and the Bnei Menashe of Mizoram and Manipur. The list is short, and every item on it is a different history.

The Bene Israel are the largest. They settled in the region of modern Mumbai, in Ahmedabad, and in Karachi, which is now in Pakistan. Over centuries they took on the Marathi language and local custom while holding to Jewish practice. Their own account places their ancestors' arrival on the Konkan coast around 2,500 years ago, following a shipwreck. That is a community tradition and this site records it as one.

The Cochin Jews are the community with the most material evidence behind it. Rulers in the Malabar region granted them copper plates recording the assumption of important positions. Copper survives, and it can be dated and read and argued over, which puts this community's early history on a different footing from an oral tradition. After a move from Kodungallur in 1524 the community established the Kochi settlement known as Jew Town, and in 1568 the Paradesi Synagogue was built there. It is the oldest synagogue in India.

The Baghdadi Jews are the latecomers and the outliers. They arrived in the nineteenth century from Iraq and neighbouring lands, leaving religious persecution behind them. The name records a region of origin rather than a single city. The Sassoon family reached Bombay in 1832 and became the community's most visible presence; David Sassoon built institutions in the city that still serve Indian society. The Baghdadi arc runs through India rather than beginning there, which is why it does not fit the same narrative shape as the Bene Israel.

The Bnei Menashe are the most recent and the most contested. Groups in the north east were required to convert to Christianity under missionary pressure in the nineteenth century, and from the 1970s members of these groups restarted the practice of traditional Jewish rites. Their migration to Israel from Mizoram and Manipur is the newest of the four movements.

Four communities, four centuries of arrival, four languages of daily life, and four different relationships to documentation. Flattening them into one category is not merely imprecise. It erases the specific thing that makes each one interesting, which is that Jewish life in India was never a single experiment repeated in several places.

One more figure belongs here, because it changes the register of everything above. The World Jewish Congress records roughly 4,800 Jews living in India in 2020, against earlier estimates of between 4,900 and 7,000 as of 1996. The communities described on this site are, in India, now very small. The synagogues, cemeteries, records and buildings are the part that stayed.

articles.title: When the government disagrees with itself
articles.standfirst: Two Indian government sources give different numbers for the same population. This page is about why that is interesting rather than embarrassing.
body: The Ministry of External Affairs bilateral brief of February 2026 records over 100,000 Jews of Indian origin in Israel. The Embassy of India in Tel Aviv records approximately 85,000. Both are Indian government sources. They do not agree.

The same thing happens with a second number. The Ministry brief records over 42,000 Indian citizens in Israel. The Embassy page records about 18,000, and describes them as mainly caregivers employed by Israeli families, diamond traders, information technology professionals and students.

The reflex on most websites is to pick one. Usually the larger figure, or the one from the more impressive institution, or whichever was found first. This site does not do that, and the reason is worth spelling out.

There are several ordinary explanations for a gap like this and none of them require anyone to have done anything wrong. The two sources may have been written at different times and not updated together. They may be counting different things: people of Indian origin is a wider category than Indian citizens, and both categories have edges that a statistician has to draw somewhere. Descendants of migrants who arrived in the 1950s are counted differently depending on how many generations back the definition reaches. Temporary workers on renewable permits may be in one count and not the other.

The point is that a reader cannot tell which explanation applies from the numbers alone. Choosing one figure and presenting it flatly would hide a real uncertainty and would give the reader false confidence. Showing both, and naming the gap, tells the reader exactly as much as this project actually knows.

There is also a practical benefit. A number presented without its uncertainty is fragile. The moment someone finds the other figure, the page that picked one looks either careless or dishonest. A page that showed both from the start is already correct.

This gap is listed among the open questions on this site. Closing it would require finding the definitional basis each source used, which is the kind of question a reader with access to either institution could answer far faster than this project can.

articles.title: Why water sits at the centre
articles.standfirst: The most durable strand of the relationship is not defence. It is the one that grew out of a problem both countries physically have.
body: Agreements signed in 1993 covered science and technology, and agriculture. The agricultural agreement is the one that kept growing. It was renewed in April 2025, more than three decades after it was first signed, and the structure built under it is now the most concrete civilian thing in the relationship: 43 Centres of Excellence approved, of which 35 are operational, working under a sixth work plan covering 2024 to 2026.

Alongside it runs a water track. A memorandum on water resources management was signed in November 2016, and a letter of intent on water technology centres of excellence followed in May 2023. In the same month the India Israel Innovation Centre for Agriculture was declared.

The reason this strand has the longest run is not diplomatic. It is physical. Both countries have arid and semi arid land, both have water they cannot afford to waste, and both have agriculture that has to produce more from less. When two states share a physical constraint, cooperation on it does not depend on either government's enthusiasm surviving an election.

This is a claim about durability, not about importance. Defence cooperation carries larger sums and more political weight, and the record shows it deepening: the first talks at Defence Minister level in March 2023, a National Security Adviser visit in March 2024, a memorandum of understanding on defence cooperation in November 2025 alongside the seventeenth meeting of the joint working group. But defence cooperation is sensitive to politics in a way that a drip irrigation centre in a district agricultural station is not.

There is a useful test for which strand defines a relationship: what would still be running in ten years if the political weather turned. On the evidence in the record, the answer is the centres of excellence. A farmer who has changed how a field is irrigated does not un-change it because of a vote in a legislature.

The open question, and it is a real one, is whether the trade track now overtakes both. Terms of reference for a free trade agreement were agreed in November 2025, and a bilateral investment agreement was signed in September 2025. If those mature, the relationship's centre of gravity moves again. The record does not yet show whether they will.

articles.title: The Haifa transaction
articles.standfirst: The largest single Indian commercial commitment in Israel is a port, and ports are never only commercial.
body: In 2022 an Adani led consortium acquired Haifa Port in a transaction valued at USD 1.18 billion. Placed against the other numbers in the bilateral record, the scale is striking. Cumulative Indian outward direct investment into Israel from April 2000 to April 2025 is recorded at about USD 443 million. Cumulative Israeli foreign direct investment into India from April 2000 to March 2025 is recorded at USD 334.26 million. A single port transaction is larger than either cumulative figure.

That comparison needs a caveat immediately, because it is the kind of comparison that gets misused. Direct investment figures and an acquisition price are not the same category of number and are not measured the same way. The comparison is useful for a sense of scale and should not be used as though the three figures were directly commensurable.

What makes a port different from any other asset is geography. Haifa sits on the Mediterranean. Indian shipping reaching it travels the Arabian Sea and the Red Sea, which is the same corridor along which the trade that brought Jewish communities to the Malabar coast once ran. An Indian consortium owning a Mediterranean port is a modern fact with a very old shape.

It is also why a port is never purely commercial. Ports are infrastructure, and infrastructure ownership carries strategic weight regardless of the intentions of the buyer. This is true of every port acquisition by any company in any country, and noting it is not a criticism of this one.

What the record here supports: the acquisition happened, in 2022, by an Adani led consortium, at a stated value of USD 1.18 billion, as recorded in the Ministry of External Affairs bilateral brief. What the record here does not support, and what this page therefore does not claim, is anything about the transaction's strategic purpose, its performance since, or its relationship to any wider corridor initiative. Those would each need their own sources.

articles.title: How to read a bilateral brief
articles.standfirst: Government briefs are the most useful documents in this field and the most commonly misread. A short guide to what they do and do not tell you.
body: A bilateral brief is a document a foreign ministry maintains about its relationship with one other country. It lists visits, agreements, trade figures, areas of cooperation, and community information. Most of the dated facts on this site come from one: the Ministry of External Affairs brief on India and Israel, dated February 2026.

These documents are extremely valuable for one specific reason. They are the institution stating, on its own record, what it considers the relationship to consist of. When a brief says an agreement was signed on a date, that is the ministry's own record of its own act. It is close to unimpeachable as evidence that the act occurred.
The mistakes people make with them are predictable.

First, treating absence as evidence of absence. A brief lists what a ministry chose to record. Something missing from it may never have happened, or may simply not have been included. Nothing on this site infers from silence in a brief.

Second, treating the framing as fact. Briefs describe cooperation warmly, because a bilateral brief is a diplomatic document and not a neutral audit. The dates and the figures are the evidential part. The adjectives are not, and this site does not carry them across.

Third, missing the negative facts. Briefs sometimes record things that are not flattering, and those are often the most informative lines in the document. The February 2026 brief records that bilateral trade fell in FY 2024-25, to USD 3.75 billion. A ministry recording a decline in its own brief is a stronger piece of evidence than the same figure from any other kind of source.

Fourth, forgetting the date. A brief is a snapshot. This one is dated February 2026, and by the time anyone reads this the situation may have moved. Every fact drawn from it on this site carries the date the brief was accessed, which is the only honest way to cite a living document.

Fifth, assuming internal consistency. Government sources can disagree with each other, and sometimes a ministry and its own embassy publish different figures for the same population. This site has a page about exactly that.

The practical advice, if you are researching this area: start from the briefs on both sides, take the dates and the numbers, leave the adjectives, note the accessed date, and archive the file. Government documents move and disappear. A brief you cannot produce later is a source you did not really have.

articles.title: What a free trade agreement actually is
articles.standfirst: Terms of reference were agreed in November 2025. That is a much smaller thing than the headlines around it suggest, and understanding the difference is useful.
body: The record states that terms of reference for a free trade agreement were agreed during the Indian Commerce and Industry Minister's visit to Israel from 20 to 22 November 2025. It is worth being precise about what that means, because in coverage of trade policy the stages routinely get collapsed into one another.

Terms of reference are an agreement about what will be negotiated. They set the scope: which sectors are on the table, which are excluded, what the working structure will be, roughly what timeline both sides have in mind. They are the starting gun, and they commit nobody to any particular outcome. Negotiations that begin from agreed terms of reference can and do fail.

After that comes negotiation, which for a comprehensive agreement between two economies typically runs for years and moves through rounds. Then a concluded text, then legal scrubbing and translation, then signature, then ratification according to each country's own constitutional process, then entry into force, often in phases with tariff reductions scheduled over a further period.

So the honest description of where things stand, on the evidence in the record: the two governments have agreed what they will talk about. That is a real step and it is not nothing. It is also several stages short of an agreement in force.

There is a second thing in the record worth reading alongside it. A bilateral investment agreement was signed on the visit of the Israeli Finance Minister from 8 to 10 September 2025. Investment agreements and trade agreements do different jobs: one protects capital that crosses the border, the other governs the terms on which goods and services do. Signing the first before negotiating the second is a conventional sequence, because investors want protection in place before exposure grows.

Against all of this sits the trade figure itself. In FY 2024-25 bilateral trade fell to USD 3.75 billion, with Indian exports at USD 2.1 billion and imports at USD 1.6 billion. Whether the negotiation reverses that, and on what timescale, is not something any source currently answers.

articles.title: The copper plates
articles.standfirst: Why one community's early history rests on firmer ground than the others, and what that does and does not prove.
body: Rulers in the Malabar region granted the Jewish community of Kerala copper plates recording the assumption of important positions. It is a short sentence in most accounts and it carries more weight than its length suggests.

Copper does not rot. A plate can be located, handled, dated on physical and palaeographic grounds, read, translated, and disputed by people who disagree about the translation. This puts the early history of the Cochin community into a category that the other three Jewish communities of India do not occupy in the same way. It is documentary evidence produced at the time by a party outside the community, which is close to the strongest form of evidence early history offers.
Two things follow, and they pull in opposite directions.

The first is that the plates support a specific and limited claim: that a ruler recognised the community and formalised its standing at a particular time. That is a substantial fact about the community's position in the society around it. Recognition granted in writing by a sovereign is a different thing from tolerance.

The second is that the plates prove much less than they are often asked to prove. They do not establish when the community first arrived, only that it was established enough by the time of the grant to be worth granting to. They do not establish anything about the other three communities, whose histories are separate. And they do not settle the broader claim, common in popular accounts, that Jewish life in India was uniformly peaceful across two millennia. A grant of privileges at one moment in one region is evidence about that moment and that region.

This distinction matters beyond the specific case, because it is the standard move in bad history: take a solid piece of evidence about a narrow claim and let it carry a much larger one. The copper plates are excellent evidence. What they are evidence of has edges.

articles.title: The exchange of 2017 and 2018
articles.standfirst: Twenty-five years passed between the opening of embassies and the first visit to Israel by an Indian Prime Minister. Then six months later the visit was returned.
body: Prime Minister Modi visited Israel from 4 to 6 July 2017. Prime Minister Netanyahu visited India from 14 to 19 January 2018. Between the two, roughly six months.

The first of those is the fact usually quoted: the first visit to Israel by an Indian Prime Minister, twenty-five years after full diplomatic relations were established in 1992. It is a real marker. Heads of government visit where they judge it useful to be seen, and for twenty-five years no Indian head of government made that judgement.

The pairing is the more informative fact. A single visit can be a gesture. A visit returned within six months, at the same level, with agreements attached at both ends, is a working relationship rather than a photograph. In the same period the India Israel Industrial Research and Development and Technological Innovation Fund was established, in 2017, and later renewed for 2023 to 2027.

There is a smaller detail in the record that is easy to skip. In Tel Aviv the Prime Minister addressed a gathering of approximately 8,000 people of Indian origin and Indian nationals. A head of government addressing a diaspora audience of that size is doing something distinct from meeting a counterpart. It treats the migrated population as a constituency rather than as background, and it connects the state to state relationship to the community history that this site documents elsewhere.

What can be said with the record in hand: the tempo of high level contact changed around 2017, and it has not slowed since. The record after 2023 shows ministerial visits in most sectors, repeated telephone contact between the two Prime Ministers across 2025 and into January 2026, and a run of agreements through 2025.

What cannot be said from the record alone is why the change came when it did. That belongs with the open questions, alongside the forty-two years, and for the same reason: the brief records what happened, not why.

articles.title: The buildings that stayed
articles.standfirst: The congregations left. The synagogues did not. What remains standing in India is the most concrete evidence this history has, and almost nobody has catalogued it.
body: The World Jewish Congress records roughly 4,800 Jews living in India in 2020, against earlier estimates of between 4,900 and 7,000 as of 1996. Set that against the buildings. There are synagogues in Mumbai, Pune, Thane, Kochi, Parur, Ernakulam, Mala, Chennamangalam, Kolkata and New Delhi. The buildings substantially outnumber the community that built them.

This is the central physical fact about Jewish India today, and it is the reason this project treats the synagogue directory as its most important dataset rather than as a tourism page. When a community becomes very small, the archive stops being paper and starts being architecture. A building can be photographed, dated, measured and protected. A memory cannot.
The Kerala pattern is the clearest case, and it is worth setting out in full because it repeats.

Kadavumbagam Synagogue in Ernakulam ceased functioning as an active synagogue in 1972. In 1974 its Torah scrolls were shipped to the Cochin National Heritage Center. In 1991 the interior and the Aron Kodesh were transported to Moshav Nehalim in Israel for restoration. The building itself is still there, closed to worship, with a business in the front room and a guardian who lets visitors see the grounds.

Parur Synagogue, built in 1615, went the same way in a different order. Its original bimah and Aron Kodesh were shipped to Israel in 1995 and replaced with reconstructions. Restoration of the building began in 2009.

Read those two together and a sequence appears. First the congregation goes. Then the scrolls go, because scrolls are the part of a synagogue that must stay with a living community. Then the interior goes, because a museum in Israel can conserve it and an empty building in Kerala cannot. What is left standing is the shell, in the place where the community actually lived, with its contents four thousand kilometres away.

Neither half of that is wrong. The scrolls belong with people who read them. The building belongs to the street it was built on. But the split means that anyone trying to understand Cochin Jewish life has to look in two countries, and that the Indian half of the evidence is the half nobody is systematically recording.

Mumbai runs differently, because Mumbai still has a congregation. Shaar Harahamim, built in 1796 and rebuilt at Mandvi in 1860, is recorded as serving roughly 100 members with daily services in a building that seats 300. Keneseth Eliyahoo, built in 1884, has a regular gathering on Sabbaths and High Holidays. These are working buildings, not monuments, and the difference shows in how they are described: condition reports rather than restoration projects.

New Delhi is a third case again. Judah Hyam Hall had its foundation stone laid on 12 February 1956 and was completed on 2 September 1956, with an annex added in 1979. It is the only building in this directory constructed after Indian independence, and its practice has adapted in ways the source records without embarrassment: the rabbi has never been ordained, the doors are open to people of all faiths, and women count towards the ten people required for a service. A very small congregation in a capital city made the rules work rather than letting the congregation fail.

Put beside a seventeenth century trading synagogue in Kerala, that is a completely different kind of Jewish history. Both belong in the same directory, and flattening them into one story about decline would miss what is actually interesting about each.

What this project can say with sources is above. What it cannot yet say is most of the rest. Five of the thirteen sites in the directory have no construction date recorded here, because no date has been read in a source this project has checked. Not one cemetery is recorded at all, and cemeteries are the most fragile category of all: unmarked, unvisited, and the first thing to be built over.

That gap is the work. A complete, sourced, machine readable directory of Jewish sites in India does not exist. Building one is within reach of a small project with a camera and a habit of citing things.

articles.title: A meeting in Mandvi, 1919
articles.standfirst: On 2 April 1919 a Bene Israel meeting on Zionism was held in a Bombay synagogue. It is a single dated line in a museum record, and it does more work than most whole chapters.
body: The record of Shaar Harahamim synagogue in Mumbai, kept by Synagogues360 at ANU, the Museum of the Jewish People, contains a line that is easy to read past. On 2 April 1919, a Bene Israel meeting on Zionism was held at the synagogue.

Consider what that date sits between. The State of Israel is twenty-nine years away. Indian independence is twenty-eight years away. India's recognition of Israel, on 17 September 1950, is thirty-one years away. Full diplomatic relations, in 1992, are seventy-three years away.

In other words, a community in Bombay was meeting to discuss Zionism before either of the two states in this project's title existed. That single fact does more to justify the sentence this site opens with, that the relationship did not begin in 1992, than any amount of argument about civilisational affinity.

It is worth being precise about what the record supports and what it does not. It supports that a meeting happened, that it was a Bene Israel meeting, that its subject was Zionism, that it took place at Shaar Harahamim, and that the date was 2 April 1919. It does not tell us who attended, what was resolved, what the tone was, whether the meeting was for or against, or whether it was one of many or the only one of its kind. A single line in a building's history is a pointer, not an account.

This is exactly the kind of item this project exists to chase. The meeting was presumably minuted, reported, or at least mentioned in the Anglo Jewish or Indian press of the period. Bombay in 1919 had newspapers, and Jewish communal organisations kept records. Somewhere there is more than one line.
Two further things make the date worth holding on to.

The first is that it belongs to the Bene Israel specifically, not to Jews in India generally. The Bene Israel were Marathi speaking, long settled, and in 1919 largely a community of Bombay and the Konkan rather than recent arrivals with European connections. A Zionist meeting among that community is a different phenomenon from a Zionist meeting among, say, a recently arrived European Jewish population, and any account that blurs the two is missing the point.

The second is that it complicates the standard periodisation. The usual story of India and Israel runs: Indian independence, then the creation of Israel, then Indian foreign policy decisions, then a gap, then 1992. In that story the Jewish communities of India appear only as objects, populations that later migrated. The 1919 meeting shows them as participants in an argument, three decades early, in their own building, in their own city.

This project lists among its open questions why India recognised Israel in 1950 and waited until 1992 for full relations. There is a companion question that is smaller and more answerable: what were the Jewish communities of India themselves saying about all of this, and when did they start saying it? The answer to the second may not illuminate the first at all. Communities and foreign ministries are not the same actor. But it is a real question with a real archive behind it, and one dated meeting in April 1919 is the thread to pull.

articles.title: The Sassoon footprint
articles.standfirst: One family arrives in Bombay in 1832. A century and a half later, a synagogue anniversary in that city draws the President of India.
body: The Sassoon family arrived in Bombay in 1832, part of the nineteenth century movement of Baghdadi Jews leaving Iraq and neighbouring lands. The Press Information Bureau records that David Sassoon built institutions in the city that still serve Indian society. The World Jewish Congress records the arrival date. Between those two flat statements sits one of the more legible stories of institution building in colonial Bombay.

The buildings are the visible part. Magen David synagogue, built in 1861 by David Sassoon in a Neo Classical style, with an elementary school for the study of the Torah on its grounds, expanded by his son in 1910. Keneseth Eliyahoo, built in 1884 by Jacob Elias Sassoon and his brother Albert in memory of their father Eliyahoo, in a Victorian style. Two synagogues, one school, twenty-three years apart, all from one family.

The pattern in that list matters more than any individual building. A synagogue serves a congregation. A school attached to a synagogue serves a congregation that expects to still be there in a generation. The Sassoon institutional footprint in Bombay was built by people making long bets on a city, and it is the physical evidence that the Baghdadi community did not regard India as a waiting room.
Two later facts show what those bets produced.

The first is about who ends up in the building. Keneseth Eliyahoo was built by and for Baghdadi Jews. After 1941 the congregation received an influx of Jews from Bukhara, Persia and Iraq. From 1948, emigration to Israel ran the other way. Today the congregation is recorded as primarily Bene Israel. A building put up by one community in 1884 is now used by a different one, in the same city, under the same roof, with the same fittings. That is not decline. It is a building outliving the specific population that made it, which is what institutions are for.

The second is about standing. The 125th anniversary of Keneseth Eliyahoo, in 2009, was attended by the President of India, the Governor of Maharashtra and the Ambassador of Israel. A synagogue anniversary drawing a head of state is a small, concrete, checkable data point about the position of the Jewish communities in Indian public life, and it is worth more than a page of general statements about tolerance.

The Press Information Bureau list of Indian Jewish contributions runs wider than the Sassoons and is worth reading for its ordinariness. Edwyn Myers gave shape to the Films Division of India. Walter Kaufmann composed the signature tune for All India Radio. Doctor Reuben David founded the Kankaria Zoo in Ahmedabad. David Abraham Cheulkar became a household name as an actor. Lieutenant General J. F. R. Jacob is recorded for his contribution during the 1971 war with Pakistan.

Notice what kind of list that is. It is not a list of community leaders or religious figures. It is a signature tune, a zoo, a film institution, a film career, and a war. These are people who show up in the history of Indian institutions rather than in the history of a minority, which is a different and stronger claim about belonging than any amount of assertion.

This project holds each of those names as a single sourced line, which is honest and thin. Every one of them is a person with a full record somewhere: a service file, a filmography, an institutional archive. Turning eleven lines into eleven proper entries is straightforward work that nobody has done in one place.

articles.title: What a shrinking congregation does
articles.standfirst: Judah Hyam Hall in Delhi changed its rules to survive. That is more interesting than any story about decline.
body: The Jewish Welfare Association in Delhi was formed in 1949. The foundation stone of Judah Hyam Hall was laid on 12 February 1956 and the building was completed on 2 September 1956. An annex was added in 1979. It serves roughly 50 local members, along with diplomats and visitors, with Sabbath and High Holiday services and bar and bat mitzvahs.
Fifty people is not many. What is interesting is what fifty people did about it.

The source records three departures from custom, stated without apology. The rabbi has never been ordained. The doors are open to people of all faiths. Women count towards the minyan, the ten people traditionally required for communal prayer.

Each of those is a real adaptation with a real cost, and each is the sort of thing that would be contested in a larger community. In a congregation of fifty, in a city where the next synagogue is a very long way away, they are the difference between a service happening and not happening.

This is worth saying plainly because the standard narrative about Jewish India is a narrative of loss. Populations fell from thousands to hundreds, communities emigrated, buildings emptied. All of that is true, and the numbers support it: the World Jewish Congress records roughly 4,800 Jews in India in 2020, against between 4,900 and 7,000 as of 1996.

But loss is a description of a quantity, and it explains nothing about what the remaining people actually did. Judah Hyam Hall is the record of a group deciding that continuity mattered more than any single rule about who may be counted, and acting on that decision in 1956 and continuing to act on it. That is not a story about a community disappearing. It is a story about a community choosing which of its parts were load bearing.

The contrast with Kerala sharpens it. In Kerala the buildings were kept and the practice moved to Israel: scrolls shipped in 1974, interiors shipped in 1991 and 1995, structures restored as heritage. In Delhi the practice was kept and the rules were adjusted around it. Two entirely different answers to the same shrinkage, and neither is obviously the wrong one.

This is also why the phrase Indian Jewish community, in the singular, is a category error that this project keeps flagging. In one country, in living memory, you have a seventeenth century Kerala congregation whose bimah is now in a moshav, an 1884 Bombay synagogue built by Baghdadis and now used mainly by Bene Israel, and a 1956 Delhi hall with an unordained rabbi and women in the minyan. These do not share a story. They share a country.

One caution about all of the above. Every fact in it comes from one institutional source, the Synagogues360 record kept by ANU, the Museum of the Jewish People, and the descriptions of practice were written at a particular moment. Congregational practice changes. If you know the present position at Judah Hyam Hall and it differs from this, an email to the corrections address is the fastest route to correcting it.

articles.title: The trouble with civilisational ties
articles.standfirst: The phrase does real work in speeches and almost none in research. A short case for retiring it, from a project that has it in its own name.
body: Anyone reading about India and Israel encounters the phrase civilisational ties within about four paragraphs. Two ancient peoples, two enduring traditions, two survivors of long histories, natural partners. It is warm, it is popular on both sides, and it is close to content free.

The problem is not that it is false. It is that it is unfalsifiable. There is no observation that would count against it. If the two countries cooperate closely, that is the civilisational tie expressing itself. If they do not, the tie is dormant, or obstructed by politics. A claim that cannot fail is not doing any explanatory work.

The second problem is that it is available to anyone. Almost any pair of countries with long histories can be described as civilisationally linked, and the phrase gets applied to India and Iran, India and Greece, India and Egypt, India and Japan. If a description fits every pair, it distinguishes none of them.

The third problem is the one that should worry anyone who cares about the subject. The phrase is often used to substitute for evidence rather than to summarise it. It is a way of asserting a relationship without having to produce a date, a document, or a name.
Here is the alternative, and it is not more boring, it is considerably more interesting.

Instead of civilisational ties, say: copper plates issued by Malabar rulers recording the standing of a Jewish community. Say: a synagogue built in Kochi in 1568 by traders including families exiled from Spain and Portugal. Say: the Sassoons arriving in Bombay in 1832 and building two synagogues and a school. Say: a Bene Israel meeting on Zionism at a Bombay synagogue on 2 April 1919. Say: recognition on 17 September 1950 and diplomatic relations in 1992, forty-two years apart. Say: 43 agricultural centres of excellence approved and 35 operational under a work plan covering 2024 to 2026.

Every one of those is checkable. Every one of those can be wrong, which is what makes them worth stating. Together they describe something far more specific than a civilisational affinity: a long, uneven, interrupted, and mostly commercial and communal traffic between two regions, followed by a modern state relationship with a very particular shape.

This project carries the word civilisations in its own name, and that is a deliberate tension worth naming. The word is there to mark a scope, that this site covers more than the diplomatic period, and not to make an argument. The moment it starts standing in for evidence on any page here, that page has failed its own standard.

There is a fair objection to all this. Sometimes the resonance is real. When two societies both have long textual traditions, both have diaspora experiences, and both organise memory around a homeland, people in each recognise something in the other, and that recognition has effects on how they talk to each other. That is worth studying.

But study it as what it is: a claim about how people in each country perceive the other, which is a question about perception, testable by asking them. That is a research programme. Civilisational ties, as usually deployed, is a way of not having one.

articles.title: Government documents disappear
articles.standfirst: The single most common way a well sourced page becomes an unsourced page is that the source moves. Here is what this project does about it.
body: Almost every dated fact on this site rests on documents published by governments. The Ministry of External Affairs bilateral brief. Embassy pages. Press Information Bureau releases. These are the right sources to use. They are also, as a class, among the least stable documents on the internet.

Government sites are reorganised. Briefs are replaced by newer briefs at new addresses. Press release systems are migrated and old identifiers stop resolving. A ministry updates a page in place, so the address still works but the content underneath a citation has changed and the citation is now wrong in a way nobody can see.

For a project whose entire promise is that every claim carries a source, that is not a minor inconvenience. It is the main long term threat. A page citing a link that returns an error is functionally an unsourced page, and worse, it looks sourced.
There are three defences and this project uses all three.

The first is the accessed date. Every source in the register carries the date it was read. That does not preserve anything, but it tells a reader exactly which version of a living document a claim was drawn from, and it tells a future editor how stale a citation has become. A citation without an accessed date is a citation to a document that may no longer exist in the form described.

The second is archiving. Any public web page can be submitted to a web archive, which stores a dated copy at a stable address. Submitting every source at the moment it is cited costs nothing and means that when the original moves, the evidence is still producible. This is the single highest value habit available to a zero budget research project, and it is the one most often skipped because it is invisible while it is working.

The third is redundancy. Where a fact appears in more than one independent source, cite more than one. Several claims on this site rest on both the Ministry brief and the Embassy page. That is not padding. It means the claim survives either one of them going down.

There is a fourth thing, which is not a defence but an obligation. When a source does die, say so on the page rather than quietly swapping in a replacement. A citation that changed is a fact about the record, and readers who checked the old one deserve to know.

None of this is specific to India and Israel. It applies to any project that builds on government publishing. It is written down here because the promise on this site's About page, that nothing is published without a source, is only as good as the sources remaining findable, and a promise with a known failure mode should say what the failure mode is.

articles.title: How to research this subject yourself
articles.standfirst: A practical route into India and Israel research for someone starting with nothing but an internet connection. The same route this project took.
body: This project has no institutional access, no budget, and no archive card. Everything on this site was assembled from documents anyone can read. That is worth writing down as a method, because the biggest barrier to entry in this subject is not access. It is not knowing where to start.

Start with the bilateral briefs. Both foreign ministries maintain a document describing the relationship with the other country. India's is published by the Ministry of External Affairs, carries a date, and lists visits, agreements, trade figures, cooperation sectors and community information. Read it whole, twice. The first read tells you what exists. The second, with a notebook, gives you a list of every dated event mentioned, which is your skeleton.

Take the dates and leave the adjectives. A brief is a diplomatic document. Its dates and figures are the institution's own record and are strong evidence. Its descriptions of warmth and depth are framing and carry across into research as nothing at all.

Read the embassy pages next, on both sides. Embassies publish things ministries do not: community information, event records, consular operations, lists of award recipients. The Embassy of India in Tel Aviv is where this project found the National Convention of Indian Jews, its host towns and years, and the Pravasi Bharatiya Samman recipients. None of that is in the ministry brief.

Expect the two to disagree, and treat that as a finding rather than a nuisance. The ministry brief and the embassy page give different figures for the Indian origin population in Israel and for Indian citizens there. When that happens, record both, name the gap, and go looking for the definitions each used.

For the community history, the reference institutions come first. The World Jewish Congress community page gives you the four communities and their outlines. Britannica gives you dated entries on individual sites. These will not be the last word on anything, and they are a reliable first word.

Then go to the museums. This is the step most people skip and it is the richest. ANU, the Museum of the Jewish People, publishes Synagogues360, which holds building by building records for synagogues including those in India: dates, founders, architectural notes, congregation sizes, and what happened to the fittings. That is where the specific, checkable, unusual facts live. A museum record of a single building will tell you more than ten general articles about a community.
For the modern relationship, the Press Information Bureau carries Indian government releases, which are dated, attributable and searchable.
Two habits make the difference between notes and research.
Record the accessed date for everything, every time. Government documents move constantly, and a citation without a date is a citation to a document that may no longer say what you think it says.
Archive every source at the moment you cite it. A dated copy in a web archive costs nothing to make and is the only thing standing between your work and a dead link.

Finally, a note on what this method cannot reach. Everything described here is published on the open internet in English. The material that would actually settle most of the open questions on this site is not: Marathi and Malayalam community records, Hebrew language scholarship, Indian and Israeli state archives, newspaper runs from the 1910s to the 1940s, and oral histories held by families rather than institutions. A project built from open web sources should be honest that it is working in the shallow end. The shallow end is deeper than most people assume, and it is not the whole pool.

articles.title: What a memorandum of understanding actually is
articles.standfirst: Most of the India-Israel record consists of memoranda, work plans, dialogues and joint declarations. They are not the same as each other, and none of them is a treaty.
body: Read the India-Israel record and you meet a vocabulary: memorandum of understanding, agreement, joint declaration, work plan, letter of intent, terms of reference, dialogue. Coverage tends to treat all of these as deals signed. They are different instruments with different weight, and being able to tell them apart changes what the record looks like.

A memorandum of understanding records that two parties have a shared intention and describes what each expects to do. In most cases it does not create obligations that a court or tribunal would enforce. It is a statement of direction, and it is the most common instrument in this record: on defence cooperation in November 2025, on water resources management in November 2016, on the industrial research and development initiative in May 2005, between India's diplomatic training institute and the Israeli foreign ministry in November 2025.

An agreement, in the way these records use the word, is usually the heavier instrument. The 1993 agreement on agricultural cooperation and the 1993 agreement on science and technology cooperation are framework agreements, and the agricultural one was renewed in April 2025. The test of weight is not the word on the cover but whether the text creates commitments and how it enters into force in each country.

A letter of intent is lighter than a memorandum. It records that both sides want to do something and intend to work out what. The letter of intent on water technology centres of excellence in May 2023 is an example.

Terms of reference are lighter still in commitment and heavier in signal. They set the scope of a negotiation that has not happened yet: what will be discussed, what is excluded, how the work will run. The terms of reference for a free trade agreement agreed between 20 and 22 November 2025 commit neither side to any outcome. They commit both to a conversation.

A joint declaration is a public statement of shared position, made together. The joint declaration on fisheries and aquaculture during the Indian fisheries minister's visit from 13 to 15 January 2026 is one. It creates visibility rather than obligation.

A work plan is the operational layer, and it is often the most informative item in a record because it says what will actually be done and by when. The sixth work plan on agriculture covers 2024 to 2026 and is the framework the centres of excellence run under. The Joint Work Plan 2026 was agreed on the external affairs minister's visit of 16 to 17 December 2025.

A dialogue is a recurring meeting. The Cyber Policy Dialogue on 27 March 2025 and the Export Control Dialogue on 27 and 28 October 2025 are not agreements at all. They are institutional habits, and habits are underrated: a dialogue that has run for years means officials on both sides know each other, which is the substrate every agreement rests on.

Finally, the investment agreement. A bilateral investment agreement, signed during the Israeli finance minister's visit of 8 to 10 September 2025, is a proper treaty level instrument in most systems, creating protections for investors from each country in the other. It is the heaviest thing in the recent record, and it attracted less attention than the free trade terms of reference, which are lighter.

The practical consequence for reading this subject: count instruments by weight, not by number. A year with one investment agreement and one framework renewal is a heavier year than one with six memoranda and four dialogues, even though the second sounds busier.

articles.title: Ajay and Sindhu
articles.standfirst: Twice in under two years, India moved its citizens out of the region by name and by operation. Evacuation records are the least ceremonial and most revealing part of a bilateral relationship.
body: Between 12 and 22 October 2023, over 1,300 people were evacuated under Operation Ajay. Between 22 and 25 June 2025, around 818 people were evacuated under Operation Sindhu.

These two lines sit in the Ministry of External Affairs bilateral brief among the agreements and visits, and they are of a different kind from everything around them. An agreement records what two governments intend. An evacuation records what one government did when the situation stopped being about intentions.
Three things make evacuation records unusually informative.

The first is that they are hard to inflate. A visit can be described as historic and a memorandum as landmark, and neither adjective can be checked. A number of people flown out of a country in a named window is a logistics fact. It is either right or wrong, and there are aircraft manifests behind it.

The second is that they reveal the size and shape of the exposed population. India maintains a substantial civilian presence in Israel. The ministry brief records over 42,000 Indian citizens there, while the Embassy of India in Tel Aviv records about 18,000, described as mainly caregivers employed by Israeli families, diamond traders, information technology professionals and students. This project shows both figures because the two do not agree.

Read the evacuation numbers against either figure and the same point holds: the number moved is a small fraction of the number present. Over 1,300 in 2023 and around 818 in 2025 are not mass withdrawals. They are the departure of those who chose or needed to leave, out of a population that largely stayed.

That composition matters for what the relationship actually consists of. The embassy's description of the Indian population is not a diplomatic or corporate population. Caregivers working in Israeli homes are the largest category named. Whatever the strategic relationship is doing at ministerial level, the daily human contact between the two countries runs substantially through domestic care work, and that is a fact about the relationship that no joint statement will mention.

The third thing is timing. October 2023 and June 2025 are both moments of regional conflict. The brief also records telephone calls between the two Prime Ministers on 13 June 2025 in connection with the conflict involving Iran, and on 9 October 2025 in connection with the Gaza peace plan. Contact intensifies when the region does. That is unsurprising, and it is worth having on the record rather than assumed, because it defines what the relationship is for on the days it matters most.

This project does not have, and does not claim, the operational detail: routes, aircraft, who qualified, how the decision to launch was taken, or what happened to those who stayed. Those things are knowable, from parliamentary answers, ministry statements and press coverage at the time. They are on the list.

articles.title: Reading the 2025 run
articles.standfirst: One calendar year in the record carries an investment agreement, a defence memorandum, a trade negotiation opening, four leader level phone calls and ministerial traffic in most sectors. That density is itself the finding.
body: Set out the 2025 entries in the Ministry of External Affairs bilateral brief in order and the year looks like this.

In February, the Israeli economy minister visits from 11 to 13 February, and a joint postage stamp pairing Holi and Purim is released. The Israeli foreign minister visits on 15 February. In March, the Cyber Policy Dialogue is held on 27 March, the director general of the Israeli foreign ministry visits from 17 to 20 March, and a deputy national security adviser visits from 11 to 14 February. In April, the Israeli agriculture minister visits from 7 to 10 April, and the 1993 agricultural cooperation agreement is renewed. Also in April, on the 24th, the Israeli Prime Minister telephones the Indian Prime Minister with condolences.

In June, a call between the two Prime Ministers on the 13th in connection with the conflict involving Iran, and Operation Sindhu evacuates around 818 people between 22 and 25 June. In September, the Israeli finance minister visits from 8 to 10 September and a bilateral investment agreement is signed. In October, a call on the 9th in connection with the Gaza peace plan, and the Export Control Dialogue on 27 and 28 October.

In November, a memorandum of understanding on defence cooperation on 4 November alongside the seventeenth meeting of the defence joint working group, the Israeli foreign minister visiting again, a memorandum between India's Sushma Swaraj Institute and the Israeli foreign ministry, and the Indian commerce and industry minister visiting from 20 to 22 November, where terms of reference for a free trade agreement are agreed. In December, a call on the 10th on the regional situation, the Indian external affairs minister in Israel on 16 and 17 December agreeing the Joint Work Plan for 2026, and an agreement for an India Chair at Tel Aviv University.
