Then January 2026: a New Year call between the two Prime Ministers on the 7th, and the Indian fisheries minister in Israel from 13 to 15 January signing a joint declaration on fisheries and aquaculture.
Three observations follow from the density rather than from any single item.

The first is that the traffic is ministerial rather than leader level. There was no state visit in either direction in 2025. What there was instead was economy, finance, agriculture, tourism, transport, foreign affairs, commerce and fisheries ministers moving between the two countries, plus defence and security officials. A relationship carried by working ministers is more durable than one carried by summits, because it does not require a leader's calendar to continue.

The second is that the heaviest instruments cluster in the second half. The investment agreement in September, the defence memorandum in November, the trade terms of reference in November, the work plan in December. Whatever was being prepared in the earlier ministerial visits appears to have landed in the autumn.

The third is the telephone record. Four calls between heads of government in nine months, on condolences, on the Iran conflict, on the Gaza peace plan, on the regional situation, plus New Year greetings in January. Two of those five are ceremonial and three are situational. A relationship in which heads of government reach each other about regional events, rather than only at summits, is operating at a different level from one that does not.

One caution against over reading. This is a single year in a document maintained by one of the two governments, and a brief records what a ministry chose to record. Comparable density in earlier years might exist and not be listed. What can be said is that the record as published shows 2025 as the busiest year it describes, and that the instruments signed in it are among the heaviest.

articles.title: Two scripts, opposite solutions
articles.standfirst: Hebrew leaves the vowels out. Devanagari builds them in. Neither is harder. Understanding why they differ takes about ten minutes and changes how both look.
body: Most people meeting Hebrew or Devanagari for the first time decide within a minute that it is difficult. That reaction is about unfamiliarity, not difficulty. Both systems are internally regular, and both solve the same problem in ways that are almost mirror images of each other. Seeing the logic is most of the work.

The problem both are solving is this: speech is a continuous stream of sound, and writing has to cut it into pieces that can be drawn. Which pieces you choose determines everything else about the system.

Hebrew cuts at the consonant. The twenty-two letters are consonants, and vowels are normally not written at all. A reader supplies them from context, from knowing the word, and from grammatical pattern. This is called an abjad, and it works because Semitic languages are built on consonantal roots: a three consonant root carries the core meaning, and the vowels poured into it inflect that meaning. Writing the consonants writes the meaning, and the vowels are pronunciation detail a competent reader already knows.

There is a vowel notation, called niqqud, a system of dots and dashes above and below the letters. It exists, and it is used mainly in prayer books, poetry, dictionaries, and material for children and learners. In ordinary Hebrew text it is absent. A learner therefore faces a script that gives them less information than a fluent reader needs, which is why Hebrew feels hard early and gets easier suddenly.

Devanagari cuts at the syllable. Each consonant letter carries a built in vowel, the short a, so the letter is not k but ka. To write a different vowel you attach a mark to the consonant. To write the consonant with no vowel at all you attach a different mark to suppress it. This is called an abugida, or an alphasyllabary, and the unit on the page corresponds to a syllable rather than to a single sound.

The consequence is the opposite of Hebrew's. Devanagari text is fully vocalised as a matter of course. Nothing is left to context, because the vowels are structurally part of every letter you write. A learner can pronounce a Devanagari word correctly long before understanding it, which is the reverse of the Hebrew situation.
Two details in Devanagari repay attention because they are where the system becomes elegant rather than merely consistent.

The first is the order of the consonants. It is not arbitrary and it is not alphabetical in the European sense. It is a map of the mouth. The first row is made at the back of the throat, the next at the palate, the next with the tongue curled back, the next at the teeth, the last at the lips. Within each row the sounds move from unvoiced to aspirated to voiced to nasal. Once seen, the grid stops being a list to memorise and becomes a diagram of speech production, worked out by grammarians long before phonetics existed as a field.

The second is the head line, the shirorekha, that runs across the top and joins the letters of a word into one connected strip. It is not decoration. It is what makes a Devanagari word a visual unit, and it is the reason Devanagari text has a distinctive horizontal grain that Hebrew, which sits on the line in separate blocks, does not.
One shared feature is worth noting because it surprises people: neither script has capital and small letters. That distinction is a European development and not a requirement of writing.

And one shared piece of history. Both traditions used letters as numbers. Every Hebrew letter has a numeric value, from alef as one to tav as four hundred, and reading words as numbers is called gematria. Sanskrit mathematics and astronomy used the katapayadi system, which encoded numbers as letters so that formulae could be memorised as verse. Two entirely independent traditions arriving at the same idea, that a writing system can carry arithmetic, is a better example of parallel invention than most of the comparisons usually offered between these two cultures.

This piece explains structure, not usage. It is an explainer, and it makes no claim about the history of either script or about their relationship to each other. There is none: Hebrew and Devanagari are unrelated systems from unrelated families, and the comparison here is a teaching device, not a lineage.

articles.title: What a project with no budget can actually do
articles.standfirst: Not compete with institutions. Do the specific work institutions are structurally bad at, which is more than it sounds.
body: The honest starting point for a project like this one is that it cannot do most of what a research institute does. No archive access, no fieldwork budget, no language staff, no peer review, no ability to commission. Pretending otherwise produces a site that looks like an institute and contains a summary of Wikipedia.
The useful question is the narrower one: what is a small, careful, open project structurally good at that a large institution is structurally bad at?

The first thing is the boring dataset nobody is funded to build. There is no clean, sourced, machine readable directory of Jewish sites in India. Not because it is difficult, but because it is not a paper, not a grant deliverable, and not anyone's job. A list of buildings with dates, coordinates, conditions and citations is exactly the kind of artefact that requires patience rather than resources, and exactly the kind that everyone else then uses.

The second is showing the disagreements. Institutions have reasons to present a settled figure. A project with no stakeholders can put two contradictory government figures side by side and say plainly that it does not know which is right. That is genuinely more useful to a researcher than a confident number, and it is easier to do when nobody is depending on the number.

The third is publishing the gaps. Most writing on this subject describes what is known. Very little of it describes, in a form you could act on, what is missing. This site lists open questions, marks entries with no recorded date as having no recorded date, and keeps a wanted list on the directory and the comparison pages. A researcher looking for a topic can read those lists as a menu. That has value and costs nothing to produce.

The fourth is speed of correction. An institution corrects on an editorial cycle. A static site with a public corrections address and a published corrections log can correct in an afternoon and show its working. Being wrong faster and more visibly is a real advantage, and it is only available to a project willing to look wrong in public.

The fifth is that everything can be given away. The data on this site is open, in plain files, in formats anyone can take. A project that produces reusable material becomes infrastructure for other people's work, which is a far more durable form of relevance than being read.

What follows from this is a discipline about what not to do. Not another general history, because good ones exist. Not another news summary, because the wire services do it better. Not opinion pieces about where the relationship should go, because there is an enormous supply of those and no shortage of people better placed to write them.
What is left is unglamorous and defensible: catalogue the buildings, date the events, cite everything, show the contradictions, name the gaps, publish the corrections, and give the data away.
None of that requires a budget. All of it requires the same thing repeated: check the source, record the date, admit the gap.

articles.title: The vote of 11 May 1949
articles.standfirst: Before India recognised Israel, it voted against admitting Israel to the United Nations. Both facts are in the record, and only one of them is usually told.
body: Resolution 273 (III), on the admission of Israel to membership of the United Nations, was adopted at the 207th plenary meeting of the General Assembly on 11 May 1949. India voted against it. India has been described as the only non-Arab state to do so.
Sixteen months later, on 17 September 1950, India recognised the State of Israel.

Put those two dates next to each other and the standard narrative of this relationship stops working. The usual telling runs: India recognised Israel in 1950, then hesitated for forty-two years, then normalised in 1992, and the hesitation is explained by Cold War alignment and West Asian relationships. That story starts too late. It begins after the most revealing act had already happened.

A vote against admission is not a small thing. Recognition is a bilateral act: one state acknowledging that another exists. Admission to the United Nations is a collective act, and voting against it in 1949 was a position taken in public, on the record, in front of everyone. India took that position and then, the following year, recognised the state anyway.

This project does not have, and does not claim, the internal reasoning behind either decision. The reasoning would be in cabinet papers, in the files of the Ministry of External Affairs, in the correspondence of the people who made the call. That is exactly the kind of material a project working from open web sources cannot reach, and saying so is more useful than guessing.

What can be said is what the shape of the two decisions implies. A state that votes against admission and then recognises within sixteen months is a state whose position moved, or whose position was always more complicated than a single vote suggests. Recognition without diplomatic relations, sustained for four decades, is consistent with a government that had settled the question of whether Israel existed and had not settled the question of what relationship to have with it.
There is a second reason the 1949 vote matters, and it is about how this site presents itself.

A site that supports the India-Israel partnership has an obvious incentive to leave that vote out. It is not flattering, it complicates the civilisational story, and nobody would notice its absence. Leaving it out is exactly the move that makes a project unciteable. Anyone who knows the subject knows about the 1949 vote, and a site that omits it is telling that reader, in the clearest possible way, that it selects its facts.

The opposite move is stronger. Put the vote in, date it, cite the resolution, and let the reader see that the relationship was not inevitable and did not begin from warmth. What was built after 1992 was built against that starting point, which makes it a more interesting achievement than if the two countries had been natural partners all along.

There is one further entry in the record that belongs alongside this one. In December 1991, India voted for the resolution revoking the earlier General Assembly resolution equating Zionism with racism. That is described as the first time India formally and openly voted in favour of Israel at the General Assembly. Full diplomatic relations followed within about a month.

Read the two votes together and the forty-two years acquire a shape. India voted against admission in 1949. India voted with Israel in December 1991. Embassies opened in 1992. The interval between those two votes is the interval this project keeps saying is the most under examined thing in the relationship, and the votes are the two ends of the thread.

articles.title: Reading India's United Nations record
articles.standfirst: India's votes on Israel and Palestine do not resolve into a simple direction. Set them out by date and a pattern appears that is more interesting than either side's summary of it.
body: This is the section of the subject most often summarised and least often laid out. Both the people who say India has swung towards Israel and the people who say India has not budged tend to cite two or three votes and stop. What follows is the record this project has been able to source, in order, with the counts where the sources give them.

The early markers first. India voted against Israel's admission to the United Nations in May 1949. India recognised Israel in September 1950. India was the first non-Arab state to recognise the Palestine Liberation Organisation, in 1974, and recognised the State of Palestine in 1988. In December 1991 India voted to revoke the resolution equating Zionism with racism, and full diplomatic relations followed in 1992.
Then the modern run.

On 21 December 2017 India voted in favour of resolution A/RES/ES-10/19 on the status of Jerusalem, adopted at the 37th plenary meeting of the tenth emergency special session. The vote was 128 in favour, 9 against, 35 abstentions. India was among the 128.

On 6 December 2018 India abstained on a United States drafted resolution condemning Hamas. That resolution received 87 in favour, 57 against and 33 abstentions, and failed because a two thirds threshold had been imposed.

On 6 June 2019, at the Economic and Social Council, India voted with Israel to deny observer status to a Palestinian non governmental organisation. The vote was 28 to 14, and India voted alongside the United States, Brazil, France, Germany, Japan, the United Kingdom, South Korea and Canada.

In May 2021 India abstained on the Human Rights Council resolution establishing a commission of inquiry into the Gaza violence, in a vote of 24 in favour, 9 against, 14 abstentions, abstaining alongside France, Italy, Japan, Nepal, the Netherlands, Poland and South Korea.

On 27 October 2023 India abstained on resolution A/RES/ES-10/21, adopted at the 41st plenary meeting of the tenth emergency special session. India's stated reason was the absence of all elements of its approach in the text. Reported vote counts for this resolution differ between sources, which this project records rather than resolves.

On 12 December 2023 India voted in favour of the resolution demanding an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages, and humanitarian access. The vote was 153 in favour, 10 against, 23 abstentions.

On 6 April 2024 India abstained on a Human Rights Council resolution calling for an immediate ceasefire, in a vote of 28 in favour, 6 against, 13 abstentions, while voting in favour of three other resolutions in the same session, including one affirming Palestinian self determination.
On 11 May 2024 India voted in favour of the resolution supporting Palestine's bid for full United Nations membership. The vote was 143 in favour, 9 against, 25 abstentions.

On 18 September 2024 India abstained on the resolution following the International Court of Justice advisory opinion, which demanded that Israel end its presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory within twelve months. The vote was 124 in favour, 14 against, 43 abstentions. India abstained alongside Australia, Canada, Germany, Italy, Nepal, Ukraine and the United Kingdom.

On 12 December 2024 India voted in favour of the resolution demanding an immediate, unconditional and permanent ceasefire in Gaza, and in favour of a companion resolution on the United Nations Relief and Works Agency.

On 12 September 2025 India voted in favour of the resolution endorsing the New York Declaration on a two state solution, in a vote of 142 in favour, 10 against, 12 abstentions. Israel and the United States were among the ten against.
On 7 December 2025 India voted in favour of renewing the mandate of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for three years, in a vote of 151 in favour, 10 against, 14 abstentions.
Now the reading, and it should be offered as a reading rather than as a fact.

What the record does not show is a country that has switched sides. India abstains on resolutions that assign blame or establish investigative mechanisms, and it votes in favour of resolutions on humanitarian outcomes, hostage release, Palestinian statehood and a two state solution. Those are two different categories of resolution and India treats them differently, consistently, over years.

The abstentions are where the movement is, and they are movement of a specific kind: from voting with a bloc to declining to vote with a bloc. Where India once could be counted on to be in the majority on any resolution critical of Israel, it now sits out a portion of them, usually the ones with an accountability mechanism attached, and usually alongside a group of Western democracies rather than alone.

What has not changed in the sourced record is the substantive position. India voted for Palestinian full membership in 2024 and for the two state declaration in 2025, both after the relationship with Israel had reached the level of joint work plans and defence memoranda.

Anyone arguing that closer ties with Israel have moved India's UN position has to account for those two votes. Anyone arguing that nothing has changed has to account for the abstentions of 2023 and 2024. The honest description is that India has separated its bilateral relationship from its multilateral position and maintains both, and that this is a deliberate posture rather than an inconsistency.

A caveat about this page. The votes listed here are the ones this project has been able to source. It is not a complete record of every Israel or Palestine related vote India has cast, and it should not be read as one. Building the complete series, resolution number by resolution number, from United Nations documents, is on the list of things this project wants to do and has not yet done.

articles.title: February 2026, and what a Knesset address is for
articles.standfirst: Sixteen memoranda, a new label for the relationship, and the first address by an Indian Prime Minister to the Israeli parliament. The label matters less than one number buried in the joint statement.
body: Prime Minister Modi made a state visit to Israel from 25 to 26 February 2026. Sixteen memoranda were signed. The relationship was elevated to what the joint statement calls a Special Strategic Partnership for Peace, Innovation and Prosperity. He addressed the Knesset, the first Indian Prime Minister to do so.
Start with the label, because labels in diplomacy are easy to over read and easy to dismiss, and both mistakes are common.

A named partnership tier is not a treaty and creates no obligations. What it does is instruct two bureaucracies. When a relationship is designated at a particular level, ministries on both sides acquire a reason to propose things that fit the designation, and officials acquire cover for spending time on it. That is not nothing, and it is also not a commitment. The correct weight to give it is: a signal about intended direction, issued by both governments simultaneously.

The Knesset address is a different kind of act. A parliament is not a counterpart government. Addressing one is addressing a country's political class in front of its cameras, which is a public diplomacy act aimed at the Israeli domestic audience rather than at the Israeli state. That it had not happened before in thirty-four years of diplomatic relations is a measure of how recent the current tempo is.
Now the number that does more work than either.

The joint statement records that the two Prime Ministers agreed that up to 50,000 additional Indian workers may arrive in Israel within the next five years, and that three implementation protocols were signed covering the commerce and services sector, the restaurant sector and the manufacturing sector.

Set that against what already exists. As of 1 July 2025, 6,774 Indian workers had arrived under the framework agreement, of whom 6,730 were in construction and 44 were caregivers. Counting private recruitment channels as well, the Indian government's own parliamentary reply put the total transferred between November 2023 and July 2025 at more than 20,000.

Fifty thousand more, across three new sectors, would change the composition of the Indian presence in Israel entirely. It would move it out of construction and care and into services, hospitality and manufacturing, and it would make labour mobility the largest single channel of human contact between the two countries by a wide margin.

It would also make the relationship legible to a much larger number of Indian families. A defence memorandum is read by specialists. A work permit is read by a household in Uttar Pradesh deciding whether someone goes.
Two other items in the joint statement deserve to be pulled out.

The first is agriculture. The statement records that 35 Centres of Excellence were operating with eight more being jointly operationalised, and that more than a million Indian farmers had been trained at them. A million is a large number for a bilateral programme and it is worth checking rather than repeating: this project records it as stated in the joint statement and labels it accordingly.

The second is water. The statement describes cooperation as focused on water conservation, wastewater treatment and reuse for agriculture, desalination, water utility reforms, and the cleaning of the Ganges and other rivers using advanced water technologies. The inclusion of river cleaning is new in that framing and is worth watching, because river restoration is a far harder problem than irrigation and a far more visible one politically.

One thing to hold on to while reading any of this. A joint statement is written to be agreed by both sides, which means every sentence in it survived two foreign ministries. That makes it excellent evidence of what both governments were willing to say together on a date, and poor evidence of what will happen. The 50,000 figure is a stated intention with a five year horizon. The honest thing to do with it is to write it down, note the date, and check it in five years.

The trade track moved in the same month. The first round of free trade agreement negotiations was held in New Delhi from 23 to 26 February 2026, covering trade in goods and services, rules of origin, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, technical barriers to trade, customs procedures, intellectual property and digital trade, with a second round scheduled for May 2026 in Israel. Terms of reference had been signed in Tel Aviv on 21 November 2025.

Put the whole month together and the pattern is a state visit used as a deadline. Negotiating rounds, protocols and memoranda tend to cluster around a leader's travel because a visit creates a date by which things must be finished. That is how bureaucracies work everywhere, and it is why counting agreements signed during a visit overstates what the visit itself achieved. The work was done in the months before. The visit is when it was allowed to be announced.

articles.title: Twenty-nine, thirty-one, thirty-five, thirty-seven, forty-three
articles.standfirst: Five official counts of the same programme, none of them wrong. A short lesson in why a number without a date is not a fact.
body: The Centres of Excellence are the most successful civilian programme in the India-Israel relationship, and nobody can tell you how many there are.
Here is the record, in order.

In May 2021, when the fifth work programme was signed, the Press Information Bureau recorded 29 Centres of Excellence operational across 12 states, producing more than 25 million vegetable seedlings and more than 387 thousand fruit plants a year.
In June 2022 the Press Information Bureau recorded 37 approved, 29 fully operational across 12 states, and 8 at various stages of construction.
In December 2023 the Ministry of External Affairs bilateral brief recorded 31 established across 13 states.
In February 2026 the Ministry of External Affairs bilateral brief recorded 43 approved, of which 35 were operational, working under a sixth work plan covering 2024 to 2026.
Also in February 2026, the joint statement issued during the Prime Minister's visit recorded 35 operating and 8 being jointly operationalised, with more than a million Indian farmers trained at them.
And the Embassy of Israel in New Delhi lists 32 centres by name across 14 states.

Five counts and a named list, and every one of them is from an official source. The temptation on a website is to pick the highest number, or the most recent, and print it as the figure. This project does not, and the reason is a small piece of method worth stating plainly.
Those numbers are not in conflict. They are counting different things at different times.

Approved is not the same as operational. A centre can be sanctioned, budgeted and announced years before it grows a seedling, which is why 37 approved and 29 operational appear in the same 2022 release without contradiction. A programme in construction always has a gap between those two figures, and the gap is a measure of momentum rather than of confusion.

Dates matter more than anything. 29 in May 2021 and 35 in February 2026 are not competing claims. They are a programme growing at roughly one to two centres a year, which is exactly what you would expect of physical infrastructure built inside state agricultural departments.

The December 2023 figure of 31 sitting between 37 approved in 2022 and 43 approved in 2026 is the one that looks strange, and it is the clearest evidence that the categories differ: 31 established is a narrower category than 37 approved.
And a named list is always shorter than a count, because publishing a list requires someone to maintain it. The Embassy's 32 named centres are the ones documented well enough to name.
So what should a reader do with this?

The rule this project applies: never print a bare number for a moving programme. Print the number, the date, the source, and the category it counts. That is four pieces of information instead of one, and it is the difference between a fact and a factoid.

The rule has a second benefit that is easy to miss. Showing five counts across five years turns a static number into a trajectory. A reader who sees only 43 learns that a programme is large. A reader who sees 29 in 2021 and 43 in 2026 learns that it is growing, and can estimate what the next number will be. The second reader knows more, and the only cost of telling them is the small embarrassment of admitting that one number was never available.

There is one figure in this cluster that this project would especially like checked. The claim that more than a million Indian farmers have been trained at these centres appears in the joint statement of 26 February 2026. An earlier count, in June 2022, recorded more than 3.6 lakh farmers trained and over 250 field officers trained in Israel. Going from 360,000 to more than a million in under four years is possible, and it is the kind of jump that deserves a definition. What counts as trained? A residential course, a day visit, a demonstration attended? The joint statement does not say, and the answer would change how the number should be read.

articles.title: The geography of a cooperation programme
articles.standfirst: Thirty-two agricultural centres in fourteen states, and not one of them in a capital city. What the map of this programme says that the diplomacy does not.
body: Read the list of Centres of Excellence published by the Embassy of Israel in New Delhi and the first thing that strikes you is the addresses. Gharaunda in Karnal. Mangiana in Sirsa. Talala in Junagadh. Chandi in Nalanda. Lunglei. Kuppam. Chinsurah in Hooghly.
These are district towns and block headquarters. The programme with the largest physical footprint in the whole India-Israel relationship does not touch New Delhi or Mumbai at all.

The distribution, as published: Haryana five, Maharashtra four, Gujarat three, Karnataka three, Punjab three, Rajasthan three, Tamil Nadu two, Uttar Pradesh two, Bihar two, and one each in Mizoram, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, West Bengal and Himachal Pradesh.
Three things in that distribution are worth stopping on.

The first is Haryana. Five centres, the most of any state, covering vegetables at Gharaunda, citrus and pomegranate at Mangiana, mango at Ladwa, beekeeping at Ram Nagar and semi-arid horticulture at Gignow in Bhiwani. Beekeeping is the outlier in that list and the most interesting item on it, because it is not a crop. A cooperation programme that has reached the point of running a dedicated beekeeping centre is one that has moved past demonstration projects into filling gaps.

The second is Mizoram. One centre, at Lunglei, for citrus. Mizoram is roughly three thousand kilometres from Israel's nearest interest and is the origin region of the Bnei Menashe, whose migration to Israel is the most recent of the four community movements this project documents. There is no reason to think the citrus centre and the community history are connected, and this project has no source suggesting they are. It is simply worth noticing that the two threads of this relationship, the agricultural and the communal, both arrive in the same small state by entirely separate routes.

The third is the crop logic. Look at what each centre grows and the programme's premise becomes visible. Date palm at Kukma in Bhuj and at Jaisalmer. Brackish water at Bhatinda. Semi-arid horticulture at Bhiwani. These are the assignments of a partner whose own agriculture was built in a desert. Israel is not being asked to advise on rice or wheat. It is being asked about the places in India that most resemble Israel.

That is the whole intellectual content of the agricultural relationship, and it is more specific than the language of technology transfer suggests. The transferable part is not farming. It is farming under a particular constraint.

The programme extends outward through the Villages of Excellence initiative, which surrounds a centre with a cluster of villages that adopt its methods. In 2021 it targeted eight states, with 13 Centres of Excellence covering 75 villages, on three stated pillars: modern agricultural infrastructure, capacity building and market linkage. The Embassy of India in Tel Aviv records 190 villages identified across 22 Centres of Excellence in 12 states.

The market linkage pillar is the one that decides whether any of this works. A farmer who adopts a new method and cannot sell the output has been given a problem, not a solution. That the programme names market linkage as a pillar suggests the people running it know this. Whether it is delivered is a separate question, and one this project cannot answer from published sources.

The Karnataka opening of June 2021 gives a sense of scale at the level of a single centre. Three centres were inaugurated together, at Kolar for mango, Bagalkote for pomegranate and Dharwad for vegetables, with a stated combined capacity of 50,000 grafts and 25 lakh vegetable seedlings a year, and about 20,000 farmers recorded as having visited them.

Twenty thousand farmers visiting three centres is the number that makes the programme make sense. Not the memoranda, not the ministerial visits, not the count of centres. A demonstration plot only does anything if people come and look at it, and then go home and change what they plant.

One limit on everything above. All of it comes from official sources describing their own programme. There is no independent evaluation in this project's record of whether yields actually changed, whether adoption persisted after the training, or what happened to farmers who adopted and then hit a bad year. Those studies may exist. Finding them would be worth more than another count of centres.

articles.title: From buyer to builder
articles.standfirst: The defence relationship is usually described by what India buys. The more informative story is where the manufacturing moved.
body: The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute records that between 2020 and 2024 Israel supplied 13 per cent of India's arms imports, making it India's third largest supplier after Russia at 36 per cent and France at 33 per cent. Over the same period India was the second largest arms importer in the world.
That is the number most accounts of this relationship reach for, and it is the least interesting thing in the file.

A supplier share tells you about transactions. What it does not tell you is whether the relationship has changed shape, and on the evidence available it has, in a direction that a purchase figure cannot capture.

Take the clearest case. The Defence Research and Development Organisation states on its own site that it is developing the Medium Range Surface to Air Missile system jointly with Israel Aerospace Industries, for the Indian Air Force and Indian Army Air Defence, and that a number of firing units have been delivered to both.

The word doing the work there is jointly. On 9 September 2021, at Air Force Station Jaisalmer, the first deliverable firing unit was handed to the Indian Air Force in the presence of the Defence Minister, the DRDO Chairman, the Chief of the Air Staff, the Chief of Defence Staff and the President and Chief Executive of Israel Aerospace Industries. The Press Information Bureau describes the system as developed jointly by DRDO and IAI in collaboration with Indian industry, capable of engaging multiple targets at ranges up to 70 kilometres.

A joint development programme is a different relationship from a sale. In a sale the buyer receives a finished object and, usually, a maintenance contract. In a joint development programme the two sides share the design problem, and the receiving country's own laboratories acquire capability that outlives the specific system.
The manufacturing record points the same way.

On 3 August 2017 Kalyani Rafael Advanced Systems opened what was described as India's first private missile subsystems manufacturing facility, in Hyderabad, a 24,000 square foot plant with the Kalyani Group holding 51 per cent and Rafael Advanced Defense Systems 49 per cent, making Spike anti-tank guided missiles and related technologies.

On 14 December 2018 Adani Defence and Aerospace and Elbit Systems inaugurated a 50,000 square foot facility, also in Hyderabad, described as the first unmanned aerial vehicle manufacturing facility in India and the first outside Israel to manufacture the Hermes 900 medium altitude long endurance drone, producing carbon composite aero-structures for the Hermes 900 and Hermes 450.
Two plants, both in Hyderabad, sixteen months apart, both majority Indian owned, both making things that were previously imported finished.

Notice the ownership split in the first: 51 per cent Indian, 49 per cent Israeli. That is not an accident of negotiation. It is the shape a joint venture takes when the receiving country has a policy of majority domestic ownership in defence manufacturing, and it means the Israeli partner accepted a minority position in order to be inside the Indian production system rather than outside selling into it.

The institutional record has moved in parallel. The first talks at the level of defence ministers took place on 3 March 2023, which is late in a relationship that had been running for thirty-one years. A National Security Adviser visit followed in March 2024. A memorandum of understanding on defence cooperation was signed on 4 November 2025 in Tel Aviv, at the seventeenth meeting of the joint working group on defence cooperation, signed by India's Defence Secretary and the Director General of the Israeli Ministry of Defence.

The text of that memorandum, as described in the Indian release, covers strategic dialogues, training, defence industrial cooperation, science and technology, research and development, artificial intelligence and cyber security, and states an aim of enabling the sharing of advanced technology and promoting co-development and co-production.

Co-development and co-production are the two words that describe the whole trajectory above, and they appeared in a signed instrument only in November 2025, years after the plants had opened. Practice ran ahead of paperwork, which is common and worth noticing, because it means the memorandum is better read as a description of what was already happening than as a plan for what will.
Two honest limits on this page.

First, defence relationships are partly opaque by design, and everything above is drawn from what governments and companies chose to announce. There is no way, from open sources, to know the proportion of the relationship that is public.

Second, this project could not verify the large headline arms package figures that circulated in 2025 press coverage, in any Indian or Israeli government source. They are therefore not on this site. If a reader can point to an official source for such a figure, the corrections address is the route.

articles.title: The trade graph nobody draws
articles.standfirst: Two hundred million dollars, then almost eleven billion, then under four. The bilateral trade series is the most volatile number in this relationship and the one most often quoted without its neighbours.
body: Put the bilateral trade figures in order and something happens that no single figure conveys.
In 1992, when embassies opened, bilateral trade was around USD 200 million, and the Ministry of External Affairs brief notes that it was primarily diamonds.
In FY 2021-22 it was USD 7.86 billion, excluding defence.
In FY 2022-23 it peaked at USD 10.77 billion, excluding defence, with Indian exports at around USD 8.4 billion.
In FY 2023-24 it was USD 6.53 billion.

In FY 2024-25 the Ministry of External Affairs records USD 3.75 billion, with Indian exports at USD 2.1 billion and imports at USD 1.6 billion, attributing the fall to regional security issues and trade disruption. The Press Information Bureau, for the same year, records approximately USD 3.62 billion.
Three observations follow, and they run in different directions.

The first is about the growth. From USD 200 million to USD 10.77 billion is a multiple of roughly fifty-four across thirty-one years. Almost no bilateral trading relationship grows like that from a standing start, and it is the strongest single piece of evidence that 1992 changed something material rather than merely diplomatic.

The second is about the fall. From USD 10.77 billion to USD 3.75 billion in two years is a decline of about two thirds. That is not a slowdown, it is a collapse, and it happened during the period in which the political relationship was reaching its warmest recorded point. Anyone using trade as a proxy for closeness has to explain that, and the honest answer is that trade is a proxy for shipping lanes, insurance rates and regional stability at least as much as for diplomacy.

The third is about composition, and it is the part most easily missed. The figures released by the India Brand Equity Foundation for FY 2025-26 up to November 2025 record India's exports to Israel at USD 1.45 billion and imports at USD 1.12 billion, with the top Indian export category being pearls and precious stones at USD 416.62 million, followed by electrical machinery at USD 243.62 million and organic chemicals at USD 63.71 million. On the import side, pearls and precious stones again lead at USD 316.24 million, followed by electrical machinery at USD 270.28 million and fertilisers at USD 85.46 million.

Look at the top line on both sides. Pearls and precious stones is the largest category going out and the largest coming in. The diamond trade that made up almost all of the 1992 figure is still, more than three decades later, the single biggest component in both directions.

That is a striking continuity, and it complicates the technology partnership framing considerably. Rough stones travel to India, are cut and polished, and travel back. The trade relationship at its core remains a processing arrangement built on an old commercial network, with electronics and chemicals layered on top of it.

It also explains part of the volatility. A trade relationship concentrated in one high value, low weight, easily rerouted commodity will swing hard when shipping and insurance conditions change, in a way that a diversified relationship would not.

Two instruments are meant to change this. A Bilateral Investment Agreement was signed on 8 September 2025 in New Delhi by the Indian and Israeli finance ministers, providing protection against expropriation, transparency, transfer rights, compensation for losses and independent arbitration. Total bilateral investment at signature stood at USD 800 million. That agreement entered into force on 4 July 2026.

And terms of reference for a free trade agreement were signed in Tel Aviv on 21 November 2025, with the first negotiating round held in New Delhi from 23 to 26 February 2026 and a second scheduled for May 2026.

Whether either changes the shape of the series is unknown, and this project would rather say so than predict. What can be said is what to watch for. If the free trade agreement works as intended, the diamond share falls as a proportion, not because diamonds decline but because other categories grow around them. If the diamond share is still the top line on both sides in five years, the agreement will have moved volumes without changing the relationship's structure.

One methodological note. All the figures above exclude defence, which is stated explicitly in several of the sources. Defence trade is significant in this relationship and is accounted for separately. Any comparison of these figures with a country whose trade data includes defence is not comparing like with like.

articles.title: Water, project by project
articles.standfirst: Of every strand in this relationship, water is the easiest to state precisely, because it lands as plant and paperwork in towns you can name.
body: Most bilateral cooperation resists description. It exists as dialogues, working groups and memoranda whose effects, if any, are diffuse. Water is the exception in this relationship, because water infrastructure has an address.

The framework first. The Union Cabinet approved a memorandum with Israel on water resources management and development cooperation on 2 December 2015, covering efficient water use, micro irrigation, recycling and reuse of waste water, desalination, aquifer recharge and in situ conservation, with a joint working group to monitor it. The Ministry of External Affairs records the memorandum as signed in November 2016.

On 28 June 2017 the Cabinet approved a second memorandum, on a national campaign for water conservation in India, described as designing, implementing and monitoring a professionally designed campaign including the reuse, recharge and recycling of water.

Then, on 5 July 2017, during the Prime Minister's visit to Israel, two of the seven agreements signed were on water: a water conservation memorandum between India's Ministry of Drinking Water and Sanitation and Israel's Ministry of National Infrastructure, Energy and Water Resources, and a state water utility reforms memorandum between that Israeli ministry and Uttar Pradesh Jal Nigam.

That second one is the more unusual document. A national ministry of one country signing directly with a state level water utility of another is a narrow, operational instrument, and it points at where this cooperation actually lives.
It lives in the states. Here is the record this project has been able to source.

Punjab signed a memorandum with Israel's national water company Mekorot on 24 October 2018, under which Mekorot would prepare a water conservation and management plan for the state, with a joint working group set up within weeks.

Haryana and Israel signed a joint declaration on integrated water resources management and capacity building on 14 June 2022, signed for Israel by the head of MASHAV and for India by Haryana's Irrigation and Water Resources Department.
Rajasthan signed a joint declaration with the Israeli Foreign Ministry on 10 December 2024, at the Rising Rajasthan summit in Jaipur, to enhance cooperation in the water sector.

Three states, three instruments, six years apart, all of them signed by the state rather than by the Union. This is federalism doing foreign policy, and it is one of the more genuinely interesting structural features of the relationship. A Centre to Centre agreement creates a framework. A state signing its own declaration creates a project, because the state is the level at which Indian water is actually managed.

Then the plant on the ground. The Embassy of India in Tel Aviv records a set of named Israeli water projects in India: desalination plants by IDE; Mekorot providing expertise to Greater Mumbai and to West Bengal; a water supply system by Tahal Group for 131 villages in Karnataka, at a stated value of USD 74 million; Aqwise, in a joint venture with Triveni Engineering, treating water in Agra; a 2017 contract taken by Ayala for an eight kilometre stretch of the Yamuna in Delhi; and Metzerplas of the Metzer Group manufacturing drip irrigation equipment in Hyderabad from 2019.

The Agra plant has a stated capacity of 160,000 cubic metres a day and supplies drinking water to a city of roughly two million people. That is the most concrete single sentence available about this relationship. It is not a memorandum or an intention. It is a quantity of water reaching a number of households every day.

The research layer arrived in 2023. A letter of intent for the India-Israel Center of Water Technology at IIT Madras was signed in New Delhi on 9 May 2023, by the Secretary of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, the Director of IIT Madras and the Israeli Ambassador, in the presence of the two foreign ministers. The centre is described as supporting India's AMRUT mission and covering integrated water resources management, urban water supply, water recycling, monitoring, water harvesting and data management. A parallel centre was agreed at IIT Roorkee.

And the direction of travel, as stated in February 2026: cooperation focused on water conservation, wastewater treatment and reuse for agriculture, desalination, water utility reforms, and the cleaning of the Ganges and other rivers using advanced water technologies.

River cleaning is the item to watch. Irrigation and municipal supply are engineering problems with known solutions and measurable outputs. River restoration is a political problem wearing an engineering costume: it requires controlling what upstream users discharge, which is a question of enforcement rather than technology. Any partner entering it should expect a much harder decade than the water supply projects suggest.

The honest gap on this page: this project has no independent assessment of whether any of the named projects performed as intended. Contracts are easier to source than outcomes. If you know of an audit, an evaluation or a critical study of any project named above, that is exactly the material this project is missing.

articles.title: The largest human channel
articles.standfirst: More than twenty thousand Indian workers went to Israel between November 2023 and July 2025. Whatever else the relationship is, at the level of people this is what it mostly consists of.
body: The Government of India describes the instrument as the Agreement on Facilitation of the Temporary Employment of Indian Workers in Specific Labour Market Sectors in the State of Israel, with an implementation protocol covering construction workers.

Accounts differ on when it was concluded. The Indian government states in a parliamentary reply that the framework agreement was signed in November 2023. Other accounts date the understanding to the Israeli foreign minister's visit to India in May 2023, before the outbreak of hostilities that October. This project records both rather than choosing, because the difference is not trivial: one dating places the agreement before the war and one after, and the two imply different things about why it happened.

The sequence after that is well documented. Recruitment centres were set up in Uttar Pradesh and Haryana in January 2024. The first batch of more than sixty Indian construction workers flew on 2 April 2024. By 22 July 2024 the Minister of State for Labour and Employment told the Lok Sabha that 4,825 workers had been sent out of 10,000 requested, the largest number from Uttar Pradesh, and stated that workers would enjoy equal treatment on labour rights with Israeli citizens, with lodging, medical insurance and social security coverage.

As of 1 July 2025, per a written reply in the Rajya Sabha on 8 August 2025, 6,774 workers had arrived under the framework agreement, comprising 6,730 in construction and 44 caregivers. Beyond the framework, approximately 7,000 caregivers and 6,400 construction workers were recruited through private channels, and roughly 220 workers returned to India, primarily because of skill mismatch and language barriers. Taking both routes together, the Indian government's own reply puts the total transferred between November 2023 and July 2025 at more than 20,000.

And on 26 February 2026 the two Prime Ministers agreed that up to 50,000 additional Indian workers may arrive within five years, with implementation protocols signed for commerce and services, restaurants, and manufacturing.
Now the part that ought to change how the whole relationship is read.

Set those numbers against every other channel. Cumulative Indian outward direct investment into Israel from April 2000 to April 2025 is about USD 443 million. Cumulative Israeli direct investment into India from April 2000 to March 2025 is USD 334.26 million. Bilateral trade in FY 2024-25 was USD 3.75 billion. Indian students in Israel number about a thousand.

Twenty thousand people, in twenty months, is by a wide margin the largest movement of anything between these two countries. If you want to know what the India-Israel relationship consists of at the level of human beings, the answer is not diplomats, entrepreneurs, researchers or students. It is construction workers and caregivers.

The Embassy of India in Tel Aviv describes the Indian population in Israel as primarily caregivers employed by Israeli families, along with diamond traders, information technology professionals and students. Caregivers is the first category named, and it is worth sitting with what that means. A significant part of the daily contact between these two societies takes place inside Israeli homes, between an elderly Israeli and an Indian care worker, over years.
That is a form of contact no memorandum produces and no summit can manufacture. It is also almost entirely absent from how the relationship is described on both sides.
Three things follow that a serious project should say out loud.

The first is that labour migration into an active conflict zone carries risks that ministerial language does not convey. The parliamentary record states that one Indian agricultural worker was killed in an attack from Lebanon in March 2024, and that three Indian nationals were injured, one in rocket fire from Gaza on 7 October 2023 and two in the Lebanon attack. Two evacuation operations have been run in under two years: Operation Ajay, evacuating over 1,300 people between 12 and 22 October 2023, and Operation Sindhu, evacuating around 818 people between 22 and 25 June 2025.

The second is the context these workers entered. Reporting at the time described Indian construction workers as arriving to replace Palestinian labourers who had lost access to Israeli work sites. Whatever view a reader takes of that, it is part of the factual setting of this programme and a site that omitted it would be selecting.

The third is that the 220 returns, attributed primarily to skill mismatch and language barriers, are a small number that points at a real question. A recruitment system that sends people who cannot do the work, or cannot communicate on site, is failing the workers first. Twenty thousand placements with two hundred and twenty documented returns is either a well run programme or an under reported one, and the published record does not let a reader tell which.

What this project would most like to add here is the workers' own account. Every number on this page comes from a ministry. None of it comes from the people counted. Oral history with returned workers, or with workers currently in Israel, would be the single most valuable addition to this section, and it is the kind of material a small project can actually collect.

articles.title: Forty million dollars and thirty-four projects
articles.standfirst: The innovation fund is small by the standards of state budgets and unusually well designed. What it does is worth understanding separately from what it spends.
body: The India-Israel Industrial Research and Development and Technological Innovation Fund, known as I4F, is a forty million dollar fund, twenty million from each side, funded by India's Department of Science and Technology and the Israel Innovation Authority. It was established as an outcome of the Prime Minister's visit to Israel in July 2017, initially for five years, envisaging funding around six projects a year of two years each. The first four projects were awarded at a conclave on 24 and 25 July 2018. The Embassy of India in Tel Aviv records the fund as having run from 2018 to 2022, renewed for 2023 to 2027, with thirty-four projects funded to date.

Forty million dollars is not a large amount of money. For comparison, a single port acquisition in this same relationship was valued at more than a billion. It would be easy to file the fund under symbolic and move on.
That would miss what the instrument is for.

A bilateral innovation fund does not exist to finance research. Research funding of that size can be raised domestically by either country without help. What the fund does is solve a matching problem. An Indian firm with a manufacturing problem and an Israeli firm with a relevant technology will, in the ordinary course of events, never find each other. They operate in different markets, read different trade press, attend different conferences and speak to different investors.

A joint fund with a call for proposals, an application window and a two country evaluation panel manufactures an occasion for them to meet. The money is the reason to apply. The introduction is the product.
Two design features in this particular fund are worth noticing.

The first is the symmetry. Twenty million from each side, and a structure in which each country's own innovation agency handles its own participants. That symmetry matters more than the total, because it means neither side is a donor. A fund where one country pays and the other receives produces a very different relationship, and usually a shorter one.

The second is the two year project length. Two years is short for research and about right for a demonstration. It selects for teams proposing something they can show working, rather than something they can investigate. That is an industrial fund rather than an academic one, and the name says so.

Thirty-four projects over roughly eight years is close to the four to six a year that the design envisaged, which is a duller finding than a dramatic number and a more reassuring one. A fund that has run at approximately its designed rate for eight years and been renewed once is functioning. Most bilateral instruments are announced, funded for one cycle and quietly not renewed.

The wider science relationship around it has a longer history. An agreement on cooperation in science and technology was signed in 1993, one of the first framework agreements after diplomatic relations. A memorandum on the industrial research and development initiative followed in May 2005. A joint research programme was launched in 2023. In December 2025 the Indian Council for Cultural Relations agreed an India Chair at Tel Aviv University, and in November 2025 India's diplomatic training institute signed a memorandum with the Israeli foreign ministry.

That last pair is a different category from the fund and worth separating. A chair and a training institute memorandum do not produce technology. They produce people who know the other country, which is the input every other kind of cooperation eventually runs short of.

What this project cannot tell you, and would like to: what the thirty-four funded projects actually were, whether any reached market, and what the failure rate looks like. Innovation funds publish their awards and rarely publish their outcomes. A list of the thirty-four with a status against each would be a genuinely useful document and does not appear to exist in one place.

articles.title: The oldest thing in the trade
articles.standfirst: In 1992 almost all India-Israel trade was diamonds. Thirty-four years later, precious stones are still the largest category in both directions. That continuity says more than most of the new agreements.
body: The Ministry of External Affairs records that bilateral trade in 1992 was around USD 200 million and comprised primarily diamonds. Trade figures published for FY 2025-26 up to November 2025 record pearls and precious stones as the largest single category in Indian exports to Israel, at USD 416.62 million, and the largest single category in imports from Israel, at USD 316.24 million.
Thirty-four years, a fifty-fold increase in total volume, an entirely new political relationship, and the top line on both sides of the ledger has not changed.

The mechanics of why are not mysterious. Rough stones move to India, where cutting and polishing take place at a scale and cost no other centre matches. Polished stones move out. Israel is a major trading and certification centre for the finished product. The two economies occupy adjacent, non-competing positions in one supply chain, which is the most durable form of trading relationship there is.
But notice what this does to the standard account of the relationship.

The standard account is that 1992 opened a door and technology, defence and agriculture walked through it. That is true, and the trade figures show it: electrical machinery at USD 243.62 million in exports and USD 270.28 million in imports, organic chemicals, fertilisers. Real categories with real volumes that did not exist in 1992.
What the figures also show is that none of them displaced the diamonds. The new relationship was layered onto an older commercial one rather than replacing it.

And the older commercial one is older than 1992 by a long way. Trade in high value, low weight goods along the routes between India and the eastern Mediterranean is the same traffic that carried the communities this project documents elsewhere. The Baghdadi Jewish families who reached Bombay in the nineteenth century arrived through commercial networks, and the Sassoons built a trading house before they built synagogues. The Cochin community's standing was recorded by rulers who valued what the community's trade brought.

This is the point at which this project has to be careful with itself, because there is an obvious and seductive move available here: draw a straight line from medieval Malabar trade to twenty-first century diamond flows and call it civilisational continuity.

That line should not be drawn, for a specific reason. The modern diamond trade did not descend from the medieval spice and textile trade. It was built in the twentieth century on entirely different technology, financing and regulation, and the people in it are not the descendants of the people in that. What the two have in common is geography and a category of good, not a lineage.

The honest version of the observation is smaller and better. Two regions separated by an ocean have, repeatedly and independently across many centuries, found that the goods worth moving between them are the ones with the highest value per kilogram. That is a fact about distance and shipping economics, not about civilisation. It explains why the trade keeps taking this shape, and it does not require anyone to have inherited anything.

That version also makes a testable prediction, which the civilisational version does not. If the constraint is value per kilogram, then the trade will diversify precisely to the extent that shipping and tariffs get cheaper relative to value. A free trade agreement, whose terms of reference were signed in November 2025, is an attempt to change exactly that ratio.

So the diamond share is the number to watch over the next decade, and not because diamonds matter in themselves. If the free trade agreement works, the diamond share should fall as a proportion of a growing total. If in 2036 pearls and precious stones are still the top line in both directions, then the structure of this trading relationship will have proved more resistant than the agreements around it.
